lessons.title: Before the Story: Wit, Riddles and Vijayanagara

activities.title: Before the Story: Wit, Riddles and Vijayanagara
activities.body:
The Vijayanagara Empire was famous for its glory, wealth and cultural achievements.

King Krishnadeva Raya ruled India from 1509 to 1529 CE.

His reign was called the Golden Era of the Vijayanagara Empire.
keyPoints: Art, literature and architecture flourished during his reign.
Krishnadeva Raya was a great supporter of learning.
activities.explanation: Now try some questions.

activities.prompt: How did learning, laughter, and clever advice shape an empire?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.prompt: A king faces a difficult court problem. How can his poet and adviser help?
steps: The king values learning, so he wants a useful answer.
The adviser is known for quick wit and humour.
A witty solution can solve the problem while making people smile.
Therefore, the king should ask him for a clever and funny solution.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Empire’s Fame
activities.prompt: What was the Vijayanagara Empire famous for?
options: Its glory, wealth and culture
Its wars, farms and borders
Its kings, rivers and roads
Its songs, trades and rains
activities.explanation: The empire was famous for its glory, wealth and cultural achievements.

activities.title: The Golden Era
activities.prompt: Krishnadeva Raya’s reign was called the Golden Era of the Vijayanagara Empire.
activities.explanation: His reign was known as the Golden Era of the Vijayanagara Empire.

activities.title: What Flourished?
activities.prompt: Which fields flourished during Krishnadeva Raya’s reign?
options: Art, literature and architecture
War, learning and poetry
Glory, wealth and poets
Warrior, adviser and poet
activities.explanation: Art, literature and architecture all flourished during his reign.

activities.title: Match the Court
activities.prompt: Match each person or group with the correct detail.
pairs: An eminent warrior and gifted poet
activities.explanation: The court’s eight celebrated poets were called the Ashtadiggajas.

activities.title: Tenali’s Work
activities.prompt: Tenali Ramakrishna served the king only as a poet.
activities.explanation: He served the king as both a poet and a witty adviser.

activities.title: A Beloved Courtier
activities.prompt: Which detail explains why Tenali Ramakrishna became beloved?
options: His clever solutions
The empire’s famous wealth
His king’s warrior skills
His court’s eight poets
activities.explanation: His clever solutions made Tenali Ramakrishna a beloved figure in the empire’s history.

activities.prompt: Tenali Ramakrishna answers a hard question with a clever joke. Everyone smiles. What does “wit” show here?
options: He has quick wit and humour.
He dislikes answering hard questions.
He feels nervous before a king.
He wants every reader to wait.

The child mistakes a dislike for the skill of answering.
Nervousness is not shown by his confident clever answer.
Delaying readers would not explain the smiling joke.

activities.explanation: The poet’s quick wit is shown by the clever joke.

activities.prompt: A poem about the empire praises its art, learning, and buildings. What does this suggest about how people saw the empire?
options: People admired its cultural richness.
People feared its lively courts.
People knew little about its culture.
People expected its learning to end.

The child confuses a praise poem with fear of the court.
The child mistakes praise for proof that culture was unknown.
The child reads the poem as a warning that learning would end.

activities.explanation: The empire was famous for cultural achievement, so admiration fits.

lessons.title: The Quarrel in the Palace

activities.prompt: How might a wise court poet help restore happiness in a palace?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Quarrel in the Palace
activities.body: Even wise rulers can face disharmony. The king quarrelled with the queen over an unimportant matter. Then he stopped speaking to her for several weeks. He also stopped visiting her because he was angry. The whole palace felt gloomy. The sad queen sought help from Tenali Rama, the court's brilliant and witty poet.
keyPoints: The king and queen quarrelled over an unimportant matter.
The king's absence made the palace feel gloomy.
The queen sought help from Tenali Rama.
activities.explanation: This card shows how one quarrel affected the whole palace.

activities.prompt: Why can a quarrel over something small make a whole palace feel sad?
steps: The king stopped speaking to the queen because he was angry.
His absence changed cheerful corridors into quiet and lonely places.
The queen felt very sad and could not solve the problem.
So, even a small quarrel can spread sadness through a palace.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Trouble with the Poem
activities.body: The king's poem contained many unclear expressions. Rama was the court's brilliant and witty poet. The king thought Rama was disrespecting his poem. He left angrily. The palace had already felt sad and lonely because of the quarrel. The queen regretted choosing that day to hear the poem.
keyPoints: The king's poem contained many unclear expressions.
The king thought Rama was disrespecting his poem.
The queen regretted choosing that day to hear the poem.
activities.explanation: This card explains why the visit ended in anger.

activities.prompt: What was the king and queen's quarrel about?
options: A palace celebration
An unimportant matter
A royal journey
A court performance
activities.explanation: The lesson says their quarrel was over an unimportant matter.

activities.prompt: The king stopped speaking to the queen for several weeks.
activities.explanation: Yes. His silence lasted for several weeks.

activities.prompt: The queen decided to seek help from ______ Rama.
activities.hint: He was the court's brilliant and witty poet.
activities.explanation: Great work! The queen sought help from Tenali Rama.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with what happened.
activities.explanation: You matched each action with the right person or event.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the order they happened.
items: The king's poem has many unclear expressions
The king thinks Rama is disrespecting his poem
The queen regrets choosing that day
activities.explanation: The unclear poem changed the king's opinion of Rama. He left angrily, and the queen regretted her choice.

activities.prompt: Which detail best explains why the queen regretted choosing that day?
options: The king believed Rama disrespected his poem.
The king calmly praised Rama's poem to everyone.
The queen enjoyed the lively and noisy court.
The king returned happily to hear Rama again.
activities.explanation: The king thought Rama was disrespecting his poem and left angrily. This made the queen regret her choice.

activities.prompt: A king hears a poem with unclear lines. He leaves angrily. What does this show?
options: He thinks the poet is disrespecting his poem.
He thinks every word in the poem is nonsense.
He wants the poet to stop writing poems.
He feels pleased that the poem confused him.

why.He thinks every word in the poem is nons: This confuses unclear expressions with complete nonsense.
Leaving angrily shows hurt and anger, not a wish to stop writing.
why.He feels pleased that the poem confused: An angry reaction does not show pleasure or happiness.

activities.explanation: He believes the poem shows disrespect, so anger makes him leave.

activities.prompt: A queen feels very sad after an argument. She visits a witty poet for help. Why does she go?
options: She hopes his clever words can help solve the problem.
She hopes he will make the king even angrier.
She wants him to write a poem about her sadness.
She plans to keep the argument secret from the poet.

why.She hopes he will make the king even ang: Seeking help does not mean trying to increase the anger.
why.She wants him to write a poem about her: The story says she seeks help, not a poem about her feelings.
why.She plans to keep the argument secret fr: She visits him for help, not to keep the argument secret.

activities.explanation: She seeks Rama because she needs help and cannot solve the problem.

activities.prompt: A king stops visiting the queen because he is angry. The whole palace becomes gloomy. What caused this change?
options: The king's absence made the palace feel sorrowful.
The queen ordered everyone to leave the corridors empty.
The palace workers chose silence because they missed the king.
The king secretly ordered the corridors to stay empty.

why.The queen ordered everyone to leave the: The fact gives the king's anger, not a queen's order.
why.The palace workers chose silence because: Their sadness comes from the quarrel, not workers missing the king.
why.The king secretly ordered the corridors: The story links the gloom to the king's absence, not an order.

activities.explanation: The king's angry absence changed the palace's happy mood.

activities.prompt: Even wise rulers sometimes face disharmony in their palace. What does “disharmony” mean here?
options: A lack of peace among people inside the palace.
A special celebration shared by all palace workers.
A wise decision made by every palace ruler.
A quiet meeting held among palace workers.

why.A special celebration shared by all pala: A quarrel does not create a happy celebration.
why.A wise decision made by every palace rul: Wise rulers face disharmony, but it is not a decision-making way.
why.A quiet meeting held among palace worker: The silence came from anger, not a planned peaceful meeting.

activities.explanation: The quarrel and silence show a lack of peace in the palace.

activities.prompt: A queen asks a witty poet to read a poem. The king leaves angrily. Why might she regret that day?
options: She knew his anger could make the quarrel worse.
She thought the poet's jokes would calm the king.
She expected the king to praise the poem.
She expected the poem to bring peace right away.

why.She thought the poet's jokes would calm: His reaction shows anger, not a wish to be calmed by jokes.
why.She expected the king to praise the poem: The story says he felt disrespected, not that he would praise the poem.
why.She expected the poem to bring peace rig: His angry leaving does not suggest that the poem brought peace.

activities.explanation: His angry reaction could deepen the sadness between the king and queen.

lessons.title: Rama’s Paddy-Seed Strategy

activities.prompt: How did Rama’s paddy seeds reveal what really mattered?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rama’s Calm Strategy
activities.body: Rama asked for time to find the right strategy. The busy court felt tense because the quarrel was unresolved. Ministers discussed ways to improve paddy cultivation. Rama claimed his special seeds would give three times the usual yield. Some courtiers mocked him, but Rama stayed calm. He said the real problem was the person sowing seeds. By yawning while sowing, he exposed the king’s mistake.
keyPoints: Rama asked for time to find a strategy.
He blamed the person sowing the seeds.
His yawning exposed the king’s mistake.
activities.explanation: Rama used yawning to expose the king’s mistake.

activities.prompt: What should Rama do when the king rejects his unusual method because of fear?
steps: The king rejected Rama’s idea because he feared harm to farmers.
Rama stayed calm and said the person sowing was the real problem.
He exposed the mistake by yawning while sowing the seeds.
The king realised that yawning did not mean disrespect.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why Did Rama Wait?
activities.prompt: Why did Rama ask for time before making his plan?
options: To find the right strategy
To stop the quarrel
To leave the royal court
To sow the paddy seeds
activities.explanation: Rama asked for time to find the right strategy.

activities.title: Rama’s Reaction
activities.prompt: Rama remained calm when the king rejected his idea.
activities.explanation: Rama stayed calm after the king rejected his idea.

activities.title: Why Was the Court Tense?
activities.prompt: Why did the lively royal court still feel tense?
options: The ministers were discussing paddy.
The king feared harm to farmers.
The court had become empty.
The quarrel was unresolved.
activities.explanation: The court was busy, but the unresolved quarrel kept it tense.

activities.title: Who Did What?
activities.prompt: Match each person or group with their action.
pairs: Claimed three times the usual yield
activities.explanation: Each group had a different response to Rama’s plan.

activities.title: The Real Problem
activities.prompt: Rama said the real problem was the ______ sowing the seeds.
activities.hint: Think about who did the sowing.
activities.explanation: Rama said the real problem was the person sowing the seeds.

activities.title: The King’s Fear
activities.prompt: The king had no fear that the unusual method could harm farmers.
activities.explanation: The king feared that Rama’s unusual method could harm farmers.

activities.prompt: The court was busy, and ministers discussed paddy improvement. Rama asked for time. What did his request show?
options: He wanted to choose his method carefully.
He expected the ministers to choose his strategy.
He wanted the court to stop its discussion.
He had already found a perfect strategy.

why.He expected the ministers to choose his: It shows he wanted to find the strategy, not wait for others.
why.He wanted the court to stop its discussi: Nothing shows that he wanted the discussion to stop.
His request shows that he was still searching for the right strategy.

activities.explanation: Asking for time shows that Rama wanted a well-chosen method.

activities.prompt: Rama said the real problem was the person sowing the seeds. What does this most likely mean?
options: The way the sower works can affect the result.
Better seeds alone will always solve the problem.
The court’s mood can change the usual yield.
The king should take over all the sowing.

why.Better seeds alone will always solve the: This mistakes Rama’s focus on the sower for a claim that seeds do not matter.
why.The court’s mood can change the usual yi: The court’s mood is not what Rama called the real problem.
why.The king should take over all the sowing: Nothing says that the king should do the sowing.

activities.explanation: Rama points to the person sowing, so the sower’s work matters.

activities.prompt: Rama claimed his seeds would give three times the usual yield. Some courtiers mocked him with sarcasm. How did Rama react?
options: He remained calm and kept control of himself.
He became shy and stopped giving his claim.
He became angry and shouted at the courtiers.
He admitted that his seeds were not useful.

why.He became shy and stopped giving his cla: His calmness shows that shyness did not control his reaction.
why.He became angry and shouted at the court: The story says he stayed calm, not that he shouted.
why.He admitted that his seeds were not usef: He supported his claim, so this mistakes calmness for giving up.

activities.explanation: The story says Rama remained calm when his claim was mocked.

activities.prompt: That evening, the king approached the queen with a softened expression. What had likely changed?
options: His doubt about Rama had begun to soften.
His anger about Rama had grown much stronger.
His wish to reject every new method had grown.
His plan to keep the quarrel alive had strengthened.

why.His anger about Rama had grown much stro: Stronger anger would not fit the king’s softened expression.
why.His wish to reject every new method had: The softened expression points to easing, not stronger rejection.
why.His plan to keep the quarrel alive had s: Nothing shows that the king wanted to keep the quarrel alive.

activities.explanation: The softened expression suggests that his earlier doubt about Rama had eased.

lessons.title: Discussing the Story and Learning Language

activities.prompt: How did the king and queen find a way through their disagreement?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Discussing What Happened
activities.body: Discussing a story means noticing what happens and why. The king wrongly believed that the queen's yawns showed disrespect, so she felt hurt. Rama waited because the dispute needed a careful plan. Later, the king accepted that he had been unfair. Humour helped reduce stress during difficult moments, while the ministers avoided the king after his confusing poem.
keyPoints: The king's wrong belief hurt the queen.
Rama waited because the dispute needed a careful plan.
Humour can reduce stress during difficult moments.
activities.explanation: The king changes his view, while Rama chooses to wait carefully.

activities.prompt: How should Rama solve the king's dispute with the queen carefully?
steps: The king wrongly linked the queen's yawns to disrespect.
The queen felt hurt because that judgement was unfair.
Rama waited because the dispute needed a careful plan.
The king later accepted that he had been unfair, so the careful approach worked.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Language Patterns
activities.body: Language clues help you discuss what you read. Words such as roared and murmur show sound. Sunlight and courtroom are closed compounds, while well-planned is hyphenated. Paddy seeds is an open compound. A possible future action can use a present tense with a present modal. The second conditional uses a simple past tense with a past modal.
keyPoints: Roared and murmur show sound.
Compounds may be closed, hyphenated or open.
Conditional patterns use different tenses and modals.
activities.explanation: The lesson names each sound, compound and conditional pattern clearly.

activities.prompt: Who wrongly believed that the queen's yawns showed disrespect?
options: The king read her yawns as disrespect.
The ministers read her yawns as disrespect.
Rama read her yawns as disrespect.
The queen read her yawns as disrespect.
activities.explanation: The king made that wrong belief, which hurt the queen.

activities.prompt: The king accepted that he had been ______ to the queen.
activities.hint: Think about his mistake towards the queen.
activities.explanation: The king admitted that his earlier judgement was wrong.

activities.prompt: Match each example to its language pattern.
pairs: Present tense with a present modal
Simple past tense with a past modal
activities.explanation: Each example matches the compound or conditional pattern given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which pair contains words used to show sound?
options: roared and murmur
sunlight and courtroom
well-planned and paddy seeds
sunlight and murmur
activities.explanation: Roared and murmur are both used to show sound.

activities.prompt: Put the story events in the order they happened.
items: The king wrongly thought the queen's yawns showed disrespect.
The queen felt hurt because of the king's belief.
The king finally accepted that he had been unfair to the queen.
activities.explanation: The wrong belief came first. The hurt followed, and the king accepted his unfairness later.

activities.prompt: Which pattern does the second conditional use?
options: A present tense with a present modal.
A present tense with a past modal.
A simple past tense with a past modal.
A simple past tense with a present modal.
activities.explanation: The second conditional uses a simple past tense with a past modal.

activities.prompt: The king calls the queen's yawn disrespectful. How may the queen feel?
options: The queen may feel hurt because the king misunderstood her.
The queen may feel proud because the king noticed her yawns.
The queen may feel calm because the king left her alone.
The queen may feel happy because the king laughed at her.

why.The queen may feel proud because the kin: Noticing a yawn is not the same as wrongly judging it.
why.The queen may feel calm because the king: Leaving her alone does not explain why she felt hurt.
why.The queen may feel happy because the kin: The story does not say that laughter made her happy.

activities.explanation: The king misunderstood her yawns, so the queen felt hurt.

activities.prompt: Rama hears the king complain about the queen's yawns. Why might he wait before acting?
options: He may wait because the dispute needs a careful plan.
He may wait because the king's complaint was already clear.
He may wait because the queen wanted another argument.
He may wait because the ministers were avoiding the king.

why.He may wait because the king's complaint: He waited because the dispute needed care, not because it was clear.
why.He may wait because the queen wanted ano: Another argument was not the reason for his careful delay.
why.He may wait because the ministers were a: Avoiding the king does not explain why Rama waited.

activities.explanation: Rama waited because the dispute needed a careful plan.

activities.prompt: After hearing the king's confusing poem, the ministers leave. Why do they avoid him?
options: They avoid him because his confusing poem left them confused.
They avoid him because his confusing poem made them cheerful.
They avoid him because his confusing poem was very short.
They avoid him because his confusing poem was about food.

why.They avoid him because his confusing poe: A confusing poem would not naturally make the ministers cheerful.
The ministers avoided him because the poem confused them.
The problem was confusion, not the poem's subject or length.

activities.explanation: The poem was confusing, so the ministers avoided the king.

activities.prompt: Hard times bring humour. Later, the king admits his unfairness. What does this show?
options: Humour can reduce stress, and the king accepts his mistake.
Humour can increase stress, and the king blames the ministers.
Humour can end the dispute, and the queen wins the argument.
Humour can fool the queen, and the king hides his mistake.

why.Humour can increase stress, and the king: Humour reduces stress; blaming ministers does not match the ending.
why.Humour can end the dispute, and the quee: Humour may ease stress, but it cannot end the dispute at once.
why.Humour can fool the queen, and the king: Humour can reduce stress, but it does not hide the king's admission.

activities.explanation: Humour reduces stress, and the king finally accepts his unfairness.

activities.prompt: A writer wants to show sound. Which pair also uses a closed compound?
options: roared and sunlight
murmur and paddy seeds
smiled and well-planned
planned and courtroom

why.murmur and paddy seeds: Murmur shows sound, but paddy seeds is an open compound.
why.smiled and well-planned: Smiled does not show sound, and well-planned is hyphenated.
why.planned and courtroom: Planned does not show sound, though courtroom is a closed compound.

activities.explanation: Roared shows sound, and sunlight is a closed compound.

activities.prompt: Which sentence uses a simple past tense with a past modal?
options: If the king accepted the truth, he might say sorry.
If the king accepts the truth, he may say sorry.
If the king accepted the truth, he may say sorry.
If the king accepts the truth, he might say sorry.

why.If the king accepts the truth, he may sa: It joins present tense with a present modal.
why.If the king accepted the truth, he may s: It joins simple past tense with a present modal.
why.If the king accepts the truth, he might: It joins present tense with a past modal.

activities.explanation: It joins simple past tense with a past modal.

lessons.title: Listening and Speaking

activities.prompt: What clever trick did Tenali Rama use at the royal court?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rama’s Challenge
activities.body: The listening story follows Tenali Rama, a quick-witted courtier in Vijayanagara. Court scholars ask him to solve their challenge, and Rama agrees. He arrives carrying a bundle wrapped in silk. The visitor has never heard of the strange work Rama named. The king laughs at Rama’s unusual explanation. The bundle is made from sticks tied with thick rope. The scholar leaves the palace in shame.
keyPoints: Tenali Rama accepts the scholars’ challenge.
His silk-wrapped bundle contains sticks and thick rope.
The visitor has never heard of the strange work.
activities.explanation: This introduces Rama’s clever challenge and the important voice patterns you will practise.

activities.prompt: Your friend asks one yes-or-no question and one wh-question. How should each question sound?
steps: Check the question type first, because the two types have different tones.
Use a rising tone for a yes-or-no question, because that is its ending pattern.
Use a falling tone for a wh-question, because that is its ending pattern.
This rise and fall in tone is called intonation, so the rule is clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Rising and Falling Tones
activities.body: Intonation means the rise and fall in your voice as you speak. Yes-or-No questions end with a rising tone. Wh-questions end with a falling tone. Listen for the difference while reading questions from the lesson. Then speak each question aloud and notice its final tone.
keyPoints: Intonation is the rise and fall in tone.
Yes-or-No questions end with a rising tone.
Wh-questions end with a falling tone.
activities.explanation: These tone patterns help you practise speaking with clear intonation.

activities.prompt: Who did the court scholars ask to solve the challenge?
options: The king
The court scholar
Tenali Rama
activities.explanation: The story says the court scholars asked Tenali Rama to solve their challenge.

activities.prompt: Rama arrived with a bundle wrapped in ______.
activities.hint: Think about what wrapped the bundle.
activities.explanation: The bundle was wrapped in silk when Rama arrived at the palace.

activities.prompt: Rama arrived with a bundle wrapped in silk.
activities.explanation: The story states that Rama arrived with his bundle wrapped in silk.

activities.prompt: Match each person with the action in the story.
pairs: agreed to accept the scholar’s challenge
asked Rama to solve the challenge
activities.explanation: Each action follows directly from the story told during the listening task.

activities.prompt: Which question type ends with a rising tone?
options: Wh-questions
Court challenges
Yes-or-No questions
Silk bundles
activities.explanation: The lesson says Yes-or-No questions end with a rising tone.

activities.prompt: Wh-questions end with a rising tone.
activities.explanation: Wh-questions end with a falling tone, not a rising one.

activities.prompt: The court scholars ask Tenali Rama to solve their challenge. Rama agrees to accept it. How does Rama most likely feel?
options: He is willing to try and solve it.
He is afraid to face the challenge.
He is angry with the scholars.
He wants the king to refuse.

Refusing would contradict his agreement to accept.

activities.explanation: His agreement shows that he is willing to try.

activities.prompt: The visitor has never heard of the strange work Rama named. What is the visitor's best next step?
options: Ask Rama to explain the strange work.
Leave the palace alone in shame.
Laugh at Rama's strange explanation.
Ask the king to send him away.

This copies the scholar's reaction, but the visitor is not the scholar.
This mistakes not knowing for finding Rama's explanation funny.
This treats not knowing as anger toward the king.

activities.explanation: Asking for an explanation helps him learn the unfamiliar work.

activities.prompt: In the story, the visitor had never heard the work Rama named. What does “strange” suggest here?
options: It is unfamiliar to the visitor.
It is pleasant to the visitor.
It is familiar to the visitor.
It is simple for the visitor.

This confuses unfamiliar work with a pleasant feeling.
This is the opposite of what the story says.
This confuses the word's meaning with the bundle's material.

activities.explanation: The story says the visitor had never heard it.

activities.prompt: Your friend asks, “Do you know that strange work?” Which intonation should your friend use?
options: The voice should rise at the end.
The voice should fall at the end.
The voice should stay flat at the end.
The voice should stop before the end.

This uses the wh-question pattern, but this question is yes-or-no.
This misses the required rise at the end.
This mistakes a pause for a tone pattern.

activities.explanation: This matches the rising pattern for yes-or-no questions.

activities.prompt: Your friend asks, “What strange work do you know?” Which intonation should your friend use?
options: The voice should fall at the end.
The voice should rise at the end.
The voice should stay flat at the end.
The voice should stop before the end.

This uses the yes-or-no pattern, but this question is a wh-question.
This misses the required fall at the end.
This mistakes a pause for a tone pattern.

activities.explanation: This matches the falling pattern for wh-questions.

activities.prompt: The king hears Rama's unusual explanation and laughs. How does the king most likely see the explanation?
options: He sees it as unusual and amusing.
He sees it as clear and familiar.
He sees it as dangerous and angry.
He sees it as simple and ordinary.

This mistakes amusement for clear understanding.
This turns a laugh into anger without any sign of anger.
This treats an unusual explanation as ordinary.

activities.explanation: Laughing at an unusual explanation suggests the king found it amusing.

activities.title: Stories and Surprises
activities.body: A narrative essay has an introduction, a body and a conclusion. It can tell a story about teamwork or a small act of kindness. In the model essay, a surprise Science quiz showed that the narrator had not revised. The teacher explained that small daily efforts add up. Responsibility means being ready for unexpected situations.
keyPoints: A narrative essay has three main parts.
Small daily efforts add up.
Responsibility includes being ready for surprises.
activities.explanation: Good stories can teach important lessons.

activities.prompt: A child packed her homework but did not revise it. A surprise Science quiz shows she was not ready. What should she learn and do next?
steps: Her packed homework does not show that she revised it.
The quiz exposed missing revision, so she scored below her expectation.
Daily revision matters because small daily efforts add up over time.
She should revise daily and be ready for surprises, because that shows responsibility.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

A small kindness

activities.prompt: The narrator studied a week earlier but had not ______.

Library stories should replace revision.

activities.prompt: A child packed her homework but did not revise it. A surprise Science quiz shows she is not ready. How does she most likely feel?
options: She feels worried because she is not ready.
She feels excited because her homework is packed.
She feels calm because the quiz was unexpected.
She feels proud because packing work counts as revision.

why.She feels excited because her homework i: This mistake treats packed homework as proof that she revised.
why.She feels calm because the quiz was unex: This mistake thinks an unexpected event must feel good.
why.She feels proud because packing work cou: This mistake treats packing work as the same as revising.

activities.explanation: This matches her worry because the quiz exposed her lack of revision.

activities.prompt: The teacher says, “Small daily efforts add up.” What does she want the child to understand?
options: The child should prepare little by little each day.
The child should study only before a test.
The child should stop trying after a low score.
The child should let classmates do her work.

why.The child should study only before a tes: This mistake limits preparation to the time just before a test.
why.The child should stop trying after a low: This mistake treats one low score as a reason to stop.
why.The child should let classmates do her w: This mistake shifts responsibility to classmates.

activities.explanation: The message tells her to make small efforts every day.

activities.prompt: A child wants to show that she is responsible for schoolwork. What should she do to be ready for surprises?
options: Be ready for unexpected situations by preparing schoolwork.
Pack schoolwork once and never revise it.
Wait for a surprise before doing any preparation.
Ask the teacher to avoid all surprise events.

why.Pack schoolwork once and never revise it: This mistake treats packing once as enough preparation.
why.Wait for a surprise before doing any pre: This mistake waits for the surprise instead of preparing.
why.Ask the teacher to avoid all surprise ev: This mistake avoids responsibility by changing the teacher's plans.

activities.explanation: Being prepared shows responsibility when unexpected situations happen.

activities.prompt: A child writes about a surprising event and the lesson it teaches. How should the child organise this narrative essay?
options: Introduce it, tell the events, then give the lesson.
Give the lesson first, then hide all the events.
Tell only the lesson and leave out the events.
Repeat the introduction and skip the ending.

why.Give the lesson first, then hide all the: This mistake puts the conclusion before the events.
why.Tell only the lesson and leave out the e: This mistake leaves out the body and conclusion.
why.Repeat the introduction and skip the end: This mistake repeats the beginning and omits the conclusion.

activities.explanation: Introduction, body, and conclusion move towards the final lesson.

activities.prompt: A child gives a classmate some needed school supplies. Which suggested topic best fits this event?
options: A small act of kindness
Learning the value of teamwork
Learning the value of surprise quizzes
Learning the value of daily revision

why.Learning the value of teamwork: This option fits shared work, not one kind act.
why.Learning the value of surprise quizzes: This option is about tests, not helping a classmate.
why.Learning the value of daily revision: This option is about preparing schoolwork, not kindness.

activities.explanation: This directly matches the suggested topic about kindness.

activities.context: A student is preparing an exhibition on the Vijayanagara Empire’s golden era. She wants to explain how court life encouraged both learning and wit. The student knows that the king supported learning, that eight celebrated poets attended his court, and that one poet was especially admired for quick thinking and humour. She also wants to mention the king’s own skill as a warrior and poet. Who can help her connect wit with service at the court, and what should the exhibition say about his contribution?
activities.prompt: Which person should the student present to show how wit became part of service at Krishnadeva Raya’s court?
options: Tenali Ramakrishna, highlighting his service as a court poet and adviser
Krishnadeva Raya, highlighting his service as the king’s witty adviser
The Ashtadiggajas, highlighting each poet’s special work as a witty adviser
The king’s literary works, highlighting them as eight celebrated court poets

why.Krishnadeva Raya, highlighting his servi: The king was a warrior and poet, but not described as a witty adviser.
why.The Ashtadiggajas, highlighting each poe: The Ashtadiggajas were celebrated poets, not described collectively as advisers.
why.The king’s literary works, highlighting: Literary works are not people and cannot be eight poets.

activities.explanation: Tenali served as both a poet and a witty adviser.

activities.context: A student is preparing an exhibition on the Vijayanagara Empire’s golden era. She wants to explain how court life encouraged both learning and wit. The student knows that the king supported learning, that eight celebrated poets attended his court, and that one poet was especially admired for quick thinking and humour. She also wants to mention the king’s own skill as a warrior and poet. Who can help her connect wit with service at the court, and what should the exhibition say about his contribution?
activities.prompt: If the exhibition must show the connection between learning and court poetry, which pairing is most suitable?
options: The ruler’s encouragement of learning and the eight distinguished poets known as the Ashtadiggajas
The ruler’s status as a warrior and Tenali Ramakrishna’s reputation for humour
The ruler’s poetry and the claim that his court had no celebrated poets
The reign’s cultural reputation and Tenali Ramakrishna’s quick wit

why.The ruler’s status as a warrior and Tena: Warrior status and humour do not clearly demonstrate learning or court poetry.
why.The ruler’s poetry and the claim that hi: The claim about having no celebrated poets is false.
why.The reign’s cultural reputation and Tena: The reign’s reputation and Tenali’s wit are relevant, but they do not directly show the required connection.

activities.explanation: This pairing directly joins learning, royal support and court poetry.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Krishnadeva Raya’s reign was called the Golden Era of the Vijayanagara Empire.
Reason (R): Art, literature and architecture flourished during his reign.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The cultural achievements during his reign help explain why the period was called the Golden Era.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Tenali Ramakrishna was chiefly remembered as an eminent warrior.
Reason (R): Tenali Ramakrishna was known for his quick wit and humour.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false, while the reason is true, but his wit and humour do not make him chiefly remembered as a warrior.

activities.prompt: Explain the main difference between the roles of Krishnadeva Raya and Tenali Ramakrishna.
activities.answer: Krishnadeva Raya was the king whose reign from 1509 to 1529 CE formed the Golden Era of the Vijayanagara Empire. He supported learning, was an eminent warrior and a gifted poet, and his court had eight celebrated poets called the Ashtadiggajas. Tenali Ramakrishna, by contrast, served the king as a poet and witty adviser. His special distinction was his quick wit and humour, and his clever solutions made him beloved. Thus, Krishnadeva Raya was the ruler and supporter of learning, while Tenali was a court poet noted especially for his witty advice.
points: Krishnadeva Raya was the king of the Golden Era.
He supported learning and was a warrior and poet.
Tenali served as a poet and witty adviser.
Tenali was especially known for quick wit and humour.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Even the wisest rulers sometimes face disharmony. A king quarrelled with his queen over an unimportant matter. For several weeks, he neither spoke to her nor visited her because he was angry. His absence cast a shadow over the palace: the formerly cheerful corridors became quiet and lonely. The queen was extremely sad and could not solve the problem. She decided to seek help from Tenali Rama, the court’s brilliant and witty poet.
activities.prompt: What is the best next step for the queen after deciding to seek help?
options: Ask Rama to help the king and queen settle their quarrel.
Keep waiting without asking anyone to help.
Ask Rama to write a poem about the unimportant matter.
Ask the king to continue avoiding her for several more weeks.

why.Keep waiting without asking anyone to he: The queen cannot solve the problem, so waiting alone is unlikely to help.
why.Ask Rama to write a poem about the unimp: A poem may add unclear expressions rather than settle the quarrel.
why.Ask the king to continue avoiding her fo: More angry silence would deepen the disharmony in the palace.

activities.explanation: Rama is the court’s brilliant and witty poet, so his help is the sensible choice.

activities.context: Even the wisest rulers sometimes face disharmony. A king quarrelled with his queen over an unimportant matter. For several weeks, he neither spoke to her nor visited her because he was angry. His absence cast a shadow over the palace: the formerly cheerful corridors became quiet and lonely. The queen was extremely sad and could not solve the problem. She decided to seek help from Tenali Rama, the court’s brilliant and witty poet.
activities.prompt: If the poem the king hears contains many unclear expressions, what is he likely to think and do?
options: He may believe the poet is disrespecting him and leave in anger.
He may praise the unclear lines and stay with Rama.
He may ask the queen to explain why Rama wrote them.
He may accept the unclear lines and continue the visit calmly.

why.He may praise the unclear lines and stay: The situation leads to anger, not praise and a friendly stay.
why.He may ask the queen to explain why Rama: The queen’s help would not change the king’s angry view of the poem.
why.He may accept the unclear lines and cont: The king reacts angrily rather than calmly accepting the unclear lines.

activities.explanation: The king sees the unclear expressions as disrespect, so he leaves angrily.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The king’s absence made the palace feel less cheerful.
Reason (R): Because he stopped speaking to and visiting the queen during his anger.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: His angry withdrawal made the formerly cheerful corridors quiet and lonely.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The queen was relieved that the palace had become quiet and lonely.
Reason (R): The king was angry and had stopped speaking to and visiting the queen.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The queen was extremely sad, although the king had indeed withdrawn in anger.

activities.prompt: How does the queen’s response to the quarrel differ from the king’s response to Rama’s poem?
activities.answer: The queen’s response was to admit that she could not solve the problem and seek Tenali Rama’s help. The king’s response was to become angry: when his poem contained many unclear expressions, he thought Rama was disrespecting it and left angrily. In other words, the queen looked for assistance to end the disharmony, while the king withdrew from the situation. Their choices therefore had opposite effects: the queen moved towards help, whereas the king’s anger helped the palace remain sorrowful.
points: The queen could not solve the problem.
She decided to seek Tenali Rama’s help.
The king thought Rama was disrespecting his poem.
The king left angrily instead of seeking help.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At the busy royal court, the lively atmosphere was still tense because the quarrel had not been resolved. Ministers discussed ways to improve paddy cultivation. Rama asked for time to find the right strategy, then claimed that his special paddy seeds would give three times the usual yield. Some courtiers mocked him with sarcasm, while the king feared the unusual method could harm farmers. Rama stayed calm and showed that the real problem was the person sowing the seeds.
activities.prompt: Why was it sensible for Rama to ask for time before presenting his strategy?
options: He needed to think before proposing a strategy while the court was still unsettled.
He wanted the king to accept the seeds without seeing how they would be sown.
He wanted to stop the ministers from considering any change in paddy cultivation.
He wanted to give the courtiers time to offer more sarcastic remarks about his claim.

why.He wanted the king to accept the seeds w: The king’s acceptance still required evidence.
why.He wanted to stop the ministers from con: Rama did want better paddy cultivation.
why.He wanted to give the courtiers time to: Rama sought a solution, not more mockery.

activities.explanation: This matches Rama’s request for time.

activities.context: At the busy royal court, the lively atmosphere was still tense because the quarrel had not been resolved. Ministers discussed ways to improve paddy cultivation. Rama asked for time to find the right strategy, then claimed that his special paddy seeds would give three times the usual yield. Some courtiers mocked him with sarcasm, while the king feared the unusual method could harm farmers. Rama stayed calm and showed that the real problem was the person sowing the seeds.
activities.prompt: Based on Rama’s explanation, what should the king do before judging the unusual method?
options: Ask Rama to demonstrate the sowing method so that the real problem can be seen.
Accept the special seeds because Rama promised a three-times yield.
Reject every sowing method in which a person yawned.
Ask the courtiers to decide the matter by mocking Rama’s claim.

why.Accept the special seeds because Rama pr: A promise alone did not remove the king’s concern.
why.Reject every sowing method in which a pe: Yawning did not actually show disrespect.
why.Ask the courtiers to decide the matter b: Sarcasm could not test the method safely.

activities.explanation: The demonstration revealed the sower’s importance.

activities.context: At the busy royal court, the lively atmosphere was still tense because the quarrel had not been resolved. Ministers discussed ways to improve paddy cultivation. Rama asked for time to find the right strategy, then claimed that his special paddy seeds would give three times the usual yield. Some courtiers mocked him with sarcasm, while the king feared the unusual method could harm farmers. Rama stayed calm and showed that the real problem was the person sowing the seeds.
activities.prompt: Suppose Rama had reacted angrily when the king rejected his idea. What would most likely have happened?
options: The king might have continued treating yawning as disrespect and missed the explanation.
The special seeds would certainly have produced three times the usual yield.
The king would have approached the queen with a softened expression that evening.
The ministers would have ended their discussion of paddy cultivation immediately.

why.The special seeds would certainly have p: Anger would not prove the claimed yield.
why.The king would have approached the queen: The softened approach followed the successful demonstration.
why.The ministers would have ended their dis: An angry reaction would not automatically end the ministers’ discussion.

activities.explanation: An angry reaction could have prevented a calm demonstration.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Rama’s yawning demonstration helped the king understand the mistake in his thinking.
Reason (R): Rama used the habit of yawning while sowing to show that the sower’s behaviour was not a sign of disrespect.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The demonstration exposed the king’s error about what yawning meant.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Rama became disrespectful when the king rejected his plan.
Reason (R): Rama remained calm when the king rejected his idea.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is false because Rama stayed calm, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: How did Rama use the yawning demonstration to expose the king’s mistake, and what did the king understand?
activities.answer: Rama noticed that the king had mistaken yawning during sowing for disrespect. Instead of becoming angry when his idea was rejected, he calmly used the habit of yawning while sowing to expose the mistake in the king’s thinking. The demonstration showed that the real problem was not simply the unusual seed; it was the person sowing the seeds. The king realised that yawning did not mean disrespect. That evening, he approached the queen with a softened expression, showing that the demonstration had changed his attitude.
points: Rama reacted calmly to the king’s rejection.
He used yawning while sowing to expose the mistake.
He explained that the person sowing was the real problem.
The king realised that yawning did not show disrespect.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In the story, the queen was hurt because the king wrongly believed that her yawns showed disrespect. Rama did not act at once because the dispute needed a careful plan. The ministers avoided the king after hearing his confusing poem. The king finally accepted that he had been unfair to the queen. The chapter also shows that humour can reduce stress during difficult moments.
activities.prompt: Rama has noticed the dispute between the king and queen. What should he do next?
options: He should think the matter through before making any move.
He should make his decision immediately, without a plan.
He should ask the ministers to settle the dispute without him.
He should wait until the king accepts that he was unfair.

why.He should make his decision immediately,: An immediate decision would ignore the need for a careful plan.
why.He should ask the ministers to settle th: The ministers' avoidance did not remove the need for Rama to plan.
why.He should wait until the king accepts th: Rama's task was not simply to wait for the king's final acceptance.

activities.explanation: The dispute needed a careful plan, so thinking before acting was right.

activities.context: In the story, the queen was hurt because the king wrongly believed that her yawns showed disrespect. Rama did not act at once because the dispute needed a careful plan. The ministers avoided the king after hearing his confusing poem. The king finally accepted that he had been unfair to the queen. The chapter also shows that humour can reduce stress during difficult moments.
activities.prompt: Why did the ministers keep their distance from the king?
options: The poem they heard was difficult to follow.
They thought the queen's yawns showed disrespect.
They were waiting for Rama to finish a careful plan.
They wanted to praise the king for his poem.

why.They thought the queen's yawns showed di: The poem, not the queen's yawns, was the stated reason for their avoidance.
why.They were waiting for Rama to finish a c: Rama's planning and the ministers' avoidance were separate matters.
why.They wanted to praise the king for his p: Avoiding the king was not a way of praising his poem.

activities.explanation: Their avoidance followed the confusing poem they had heard.

activities.prompt: What made one young officer’s courage echo through history?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Remembering Major Somnath Sharma
activities.body: Major Somnath Sharma was India’s first Param Vir Chakra recipient. His bravery and sacrifice inspired generations of people. In Kashmir Valley, he led 90 men on a mission to protect Srinagar airport. They stopped about 500 infiltrators. The invaders wanted to capture Srinagar and strike newly independent India. His legacy of courage and devotion to the nation remains alive.
keyPoints: India’s first Param Vir Chakra recipient
Led 90 men to protect Srinagar airport
His courage inspired generations
activities.explanation: His courage inspired generations, and his mission protected Srinagar airport.

activities.prompt: A child sees 90 men protecting an airport from about 500 infiltrators. Why is this brave?
steps: In Kashmir Valley, capturing Srinagar would help strike newly independent India.
Major Sharma led 90 men to protect the airport from danger.
The 90 men stopped about 500 infiltrators, showing great courage.
Because his courage inspired generations, the mission deserves our lasting tribute.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Major Somnath Sharma led ______ men on the mission.
activities.hint: How many men did he lead?
activities.explanation: Major Somnath Sharma led 90 men on the mission.

activities.prompt: The invaders wanted to capture Srinagar and strike newly independent India.
activities.explanation: Capturing Srinagar would help the invaders strike newly independent India.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct detail.
pairs: India’s first Param Vir Chakra recipient
Inspired by his bravery and sacrifice
activities.explanation: Each clue connects Sharma’s honour, courage, setting, and mission.

activities.prompt: What did the 90 men stop?
options: About 500 infiltrators
Major Somnath Sharma
Srinagar airport
Kashmir Valley
activities.explanation: The 90 men stopped about 500 infiltrators from taking Srinagar.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the correct order.
items: The invaders wanted to capture Srinagar and strike India.
The battle ended with echoes of courage.
activities.explanation: The invasion threat led to Sharma’s mission and the battle.

activities.prompt: Why did the invaders want to capture Srinagar?
options: To strike newly independent India
To protect Srinagar airport
To honour Sharma’s courage
To stop the infiltrators
activities.explanation: The invaders wanted to capture Srinagar and strike newly independent India.

activities.prompt: In Kashmir Valley, Major Sharma led 90 men against about 500 infiltrators. What did this show?
options: He showed courage and strong leadership.
He felt no fear during the battle.
He acted mainly to win personal fame.
He believed the mission would be easy.

This mistake thinks courage means feeling no fear.
This mistake thinks service to the nation came from seeking fame.
This mistake thinks a dangerous mission was simple.

activities.explanation: Leading 90 men against a larger force shows great courage.

activities.prompt: The invaders wanted to capture Srinagar and strike newly independent India. Why was stopping them important?
options: It helped protect Srinagar and newly independent India.
It helped the invaders capture their wanted city.
It made the airport safer for arriving visitors.
It gave the soldiers a wish for personal fame.

why.It helped the invaders capture their wan: This mistake mistakes protection for helping the invaders.
why.It made the airport safer for arriving v: This mistake mistakes an airport target for a place for visitors.
why.It gave the soldiers a wish for personal: This mistake mistakes national service for a wish for fame.

activities.explanation: Stopping them protected Srinagar and newly independent India.

activities.prompt: Major Somnath Sharma was India's first Param Vir Chakra recipient. Why is this honour a tribute to him?
options: His courage and sacrifice greatly served the nation.
His mission was easy and without any danger.
He received more honours than every other soldier.
He fought in every battle of that time.

why.His mission was easy and without any dan: This mistake thinks his dangerous mission was easy.
why.He received more honours than every othe: This mistake thinks being first means receiving every honour.
This mistake thinks one great act means fighting every battle.

activities.explanation: His courage and sacrifice inspired generations and served the nation.

activities.prompt: A poem says, “His name is fixed in history's annals.” What does it imply?
options: His courage will be remembered for a long time.
His name was written on a school wall.
He won every battle in all of history.
He spent his life writing history books.

This mistake thinks annals means a school wall.
This mistake thinks being remembered means winning every battle.
This mistake confuses being remembered with writing history.

activities.explanation: Being fixed in history's annals means lasting remembrance.

lessons.title: Operation Gulmarg

activities.prompt: How did India’s troops reach Srinagar during the fighting in Kashmir?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Was Operation Gulmarg?
activities.body: Operation Gulmarg was Pakistan's plan to take the Kashmir Valley. Invaders are fighters sent from outside. Pakistan trained and equipped around 1000 of them. They knew the mountain passes and local terrain well. They planned to make people rise against the government. Then they would capture the territory. Pakistan had agreed with Hari Singh not to attack Jammu and Kashmir.
keyPoints: Pakistan trained and equipped around 1000 invaders.
The invaders knew the local terrain well.
The plan was to cause a revolt and capture the territory.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the plan and the people who carried it out.

activities.prompt: Your class plans a mountain trip. Why choose a guide who knows the paths?
steps: A guide who knows the paths can help a mountain group travel.
The invaders knew the mountain passes and local terrain well.
Capturing Kashmir would give them control of important passes and peaks.
Therefore, their knowledge helped them pursue their capture plan.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Operation Gulmarg was launched on 22 September 1947.
activities.explanation: It was launched on 22 October 1947. September was the wrong month.

activities.prompt: Operation Gulmarg was launched on ______ October 1947.
activities.hint: Use the date given in your lesson.
activities.explanation: The operation began on 22 October 1947.

activities.prompt: Match each step of the plan with its action.
activities.explanation: The plan began with a revolt. The invaders would then overthrow the government and capture the territory.

activities.prompt: Why did capturing Kashmir matter to the invaders?
options: It gave control of important passes, peaks and rivers.
It gave control of distant passes, peaks and rivers.
It gave control of important passes, plains and roads.
It gave control of small passes, peaks and rivers.
activities.explanation: Capturing Kashmir would give them control of important passes, peaks and rivers.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Jammu and Kashmir became part of India
Indian troops sent to defend Kashmir
activities.explanation: August began the events leading to Badgam. The other events happened from 22 to 31 October.

activities.prompt: Which statement about D Company is correct?
options: It flew to Srinagar on 31 October.
It flew to Jammu on 27 October.
It walked to Srinagar on 31 October.
It flew to Delhi on 22 October.
activities.explanation: It flew to Srinagar on 31 October. This was D Company of the 4th Kumaon Battalion.

activities.prompt: Pakistan launched Operation Gulmarg to annex the Kashmir Valley. What does “annex” mean here?
options: To take control of the territory
To defend the territory from attack
To return the territory to its rulers
To borrow the territory for a short time

why.To defend the territory from attack: This mistake treats annex as protecting territory from attack.
why.To return the territory to its rulers: This mistake treats annex as giving territory back.
why.To borrow the territory for a short time: This mistake treats annex as only borrowing territory briefly.

activities.explanation: This is correct because annex means taking control of territory.

activities.prompt: Pakistan agreed not to attack Jammu and Kashmir. Operation Gulmarg later began. How might Hari Singh feel?
options: Hari Singh may feel that his trust was broken.
Hari Singh may think that Pakistan kept its promise.
Hari Singh may feel that the agreement helped him.
Hari Singh may think that no attack was planned.

why.Hari Singh may think that Pakistan kept: This wrongly assumes the agreement prevented the operation.
why.Hari Singh may feel that the agreement h: This wrongly treats the agreement as helping Pakistan.
why.Hari Singh may think that no attack was: This wrongly assumes the operation was never planned.

activities.explanation: The operation began after Pakistan had agreed not to attack.

activities.prompt: Around 1000 invaders were trained and equipped. They also knew the passes and terrain. What can you infer?
options: Their preparation included both training and local knowledge.
Their preparation included training but not local knowledge.
Their preparation included local knowledge but not training.
Their preparation included numbers but no useful knowledge.

why.Their preparation included training but: This overlooks that they also knew the local terrain.
why.Their preparation included local knowled: This overlooks that the invaders were trained and equipped.
why.Their preparation included numbers but n: This wrongly treats numbers as their only useful preparation.

activities.explanation: Training and terrain knowledge were both part of their preparation.

activities.prompt: The land route to Srinagar was badly damaged. Indian troops were sent there. Why were they taken by air?
options: The damaged road made land travel too hard.
The mountains made air travel too dangerous.
The troops wanted to avoid meeting local people.
Air travel was shorter than the land route.

why.The mountains made air travel too danger: This wrongly blames the mountains rather than the damaged route.
why.The troops wanted to avoid meeting local: This wrongly guesses that troops wanted to avoid local people.
why.Air travel was shorter than the land rou: This wrongly treats distance as the reason for choosing air travel.

activities.explanation: The damaged land route made reaching Srinagar by road hard.

activities.prompt: Invaders planned to cause a revolt, then capture the territory. What might they hope local people will do?
options: They may rise up against the existing government.
They may leave Kashmir for another country.
They may ask India to send more troops.
They may repair the damaged mountain roads themselves.

why.They may leave Kashmir for another count: This wrongly assumes their plan was to make people leave.
This wrongly assumes their plan depended on more Indian troops.
why.They may repair the damaged mountain roa: This wrongly turns the revolt plan into a road repair plan.

activities.explanation: Causing a revolt needed local people to rise against the government.

activities.prompt: Pakistan launched Operation Gulmarg on 22 October. Kashmir became part of India on 26 October. What can you infer?
options: Indian troops were sent after the operation began.
Indian troops were sent before the operation began.
Indian troops arrived before Kashmir joined India.
The operation began after troops reached Srinagar.

why.Indian troops were sent before the opera: This reverses the order of the operation and troop departure.
why.Indian troops arrived before Kashmir joi: This reverses the order of Kashmir joining India and troop arrival.
why.The operation began after troops reached: This puts the operation after D Company reached Srinagar.

activities.explanation: India sent troops on 27 October, after the 22 October launch.

lessons.title: Patrol at Badgam

activities.prompt: What would make a leader return to danger with his company?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Major Somnath and the Badgam Patrol
activities.body: Major Somnath Sharma had his left hand in plaster, but he joined his company. He refused to let his men enter action without him. His words showed commitment to his men and country. The tribal rumours had no sound basis. Badgam was less than 5 kilometres from Srinagar airport. Controlling it could protect troops and allow supplies to arrive. The enemy entered in small groups to avoid detection. Companies patrolled Badgam.
keyPoints: Major Somnath joined despite his plastered hand.
He demanded that his men not enter action without him.
Patrolling Badgam protected troops and supplies.
activities.explanation: The lesson links his commitment with the patrol's purpose.

activities.prompt: Why did Major Somnath Sharma and his soldiers patrol Badgam?
steps: Badgam was near Srinagar airport, so supplies could reach forces by air.
Enemy groups entered in small groups, so patrols could check for threats.
D Company stayed last, so Major led 90 soldiers against danger.
The attack met stiff resistance, so patrol could protect troops and supplies.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why did Major Somnath insist on joining his company?
options: His commitment to his men and country
His wish to leave his men alone
His plan to stay near the airport
His interest in the tribal rumours
activities.explanation: His words showed strong commitment to his men and country.

activities.prompt: Why was controlling Badgam important for the Indian troops?
options: To protect troops and help supplies arrive
To stop supplies from reaching Indian forces
To keep Indian forces away from the airport
To bring larger enemy groups into Badgam
activities.explanation: Controlling Badgam would protect Indian troops and allow supplies to arrive.

activities.prompt: On 3 November, several companies were sent to patrol and assess ______ around Badgam.
activities.hint: What were the patrols checking?
activities.explanation: Several companies patrolled Badgam and assessed the threats there.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its detail from the lesson.
pairs: Could reach Indian forces by air
activities.explanation: These details describe the location, departure, supply route and resistance.

activities.prompt: Which statement fits the lesson best?
options: The rumours had no basis, and enemies avoided detection.
The rumours were true, and enemies entered in large groups.
The rumours had no basis, and enemies entered in large groups.
The valley was noisy, and enemies entered in large groups.
activities.explanation: The rumours had no sound basis. The enemy entered in small groups to avoid detection.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Companies were sent to patrol Badgam.
The valley remained silent throughout the day.
The enemy's first attack met stiff resistance.
activities.explanation: The lesson moves from the patrol to the silent day, departure and resistance.

activities.prompt: Major's hand is hurt, but his men could patrol alone. Why must he stay?
options: He feels responsible for his men and country.
He wants to show that injuries never matter.
He thinks his men cannot act without him.
He hopes the patrol will end much sooner.

why.He wants to show that injuries never mat: He stayed for his men and country, not to show off.
why.He thinks his men cannot act without him: He wanted to lead beside them, not because they could not act.
why.He hopes the patrol will end much sooner: Nothing suggests that he wanted the patrol to end sooner.

activities.explanation: Joining his company and refusing to leave show deep responsibility.

activities.prompt: Patrol leaders hear a rumour about tribal movement near Badgam. What should they do?
options: Check for proof, because the rumour has no basis.
Act at once, because every rumour predicts danger.
Tell everyone, because sharing news makes it true.
Stop all patrols, because rumours always end patrols.

why.Act at once, because every rumour predic: This mistake treats an unsupported rumour as real evidence.
why.Tell everyone, because sharing news make: This mistake thinks repeating a rumour can make it true.
why.Stop all patrols, because rumours always: This mistake lets a baseless rumour stop the patrol.

activities.explanation: The rumour had no sound basis, so proof was needed.

activities.prompt: Badgam is close to Srinagar airport. Why might controlling it help the army?
options: It can protect troops and let supplies reach them.
It can make the airport and all roads useless.
It can remove the need to guard nearby forces.
It can stop supplies from reaching Indian troops.

why.It can make the airport and all roads us: The area's location made control helpful, not harmful.
why.It can remove the need to guard nearby f: This mistake says troops and supplies would not need protection.
why.It can stop supplies from reaching India: This mistake reverses the result of controlling Badgam.

activities.explanation: Control could protect troops and keep supplies reaching them.

activities.prompt: Enemy soldiers enter Badgam in small groups. Why might this help their plan?
options: Small groups are less likely to be noticed.
Small groups can always cross much larger mountains.
Small groups need no supplies during their movement.
Small groups make every patrol stop and leave.

why.Small groups can always cross much large: Their small size did not let them cross any mountains.
why.Small groups need no supplies during the: Their small size did not remove their need for supplies.
why.Small groups make every patrol stop and: Small groups did not make patrols leave the area.

activities.explanation: Small groups reduce the chance of being noticed by patrols.

activities.prompt: The valley stays silent all day during the patrol. What may leaders suspect?
options: Enemy may be moving carefully to avoid detection.
Every nearby village has already been emptied.
Airport supplies have stopped reaching Badgam.
All enemy groups have decided to leave forever.

why.Every nearby village has already been em: Silence alone cannot show that every village was empty.
why.Airport supplies have stopped reaching B: Silence alone cannot show that airport supplies had stopped.
why.All enemy groups have decided to leave f: Silence alone cannot show that every enemy group had left.

activities.explanation: Small enemy groups tried to avoid detection, so silence could hide them.

lessons.title: The Battle of Badgam

activities.prompt: How did a small team protect an airfield against a much larger force?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Facing the Attack
activities.body: Major Somnath Sharma understood that the first attack was only a distraction. A much larger attack came from another side. He and his 90 soldiers faced about 500 invaders. He requested air strikes and placed ground panels to guide the aircraft towards its target. The strikes hit the tribal invaders. D Company held its ground despite heavy fire. Sharma directed fire, filled gunners’ magazines and encouraged his soldiers.
keyPoints: The first attack was a distraction.
Sharma requested air strikes and guided the aircraft.
He encouraged his soldiers to hold their ground.
activities.explanation: Sharma used clear actions and words to help his soldiers hold their ground.

activities.prompt: The first attack is only a distraction. How should the defenders prepare for the real danger?
steps: The first attack is only a distraction, so danger may come later.
The larger attack threatens the airfield, town and wider valley.
With ninety soldiers against five hundred invaders, ground defence alone is hard.
Defenders can use guided air strikes to hit the larger enemy force.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Major Somnath Sharma understand about the first attack?
options: The main attack
Only a distraction
A warning sign
A final victory
activities.explanation: The first attack was only a distraction. A much larger attack came from another side.

activities.prompt: The invaders wanted to capture Srinagar airfield and the ______ area.
activities.hint: This word describes the land around the airfield.
activities.explanation: The invaders wanted to capture Srinagar airfield and the surrounding area.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the attack with what happened.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an event with its role in the battle.

activities.prompt: Why did Major Somnath Sharma lay out ground panels?
options: Carry soldiers towards safety
Guard town against another attack
Guide aircraft towards the target
Fill gunners’ empty magazines
activities.explanation: The panels guided the aircraft towards its target, helping the air strikes.

activities.prompt: Put these actions in the order they happened.
activities.explanation: Sharma assessed the battle, requested support and guided the air strikes.

activities.prompt: What did Sharma do while heavy fire continued?
options: He stopped fighting and left the valley
He helped invaders capture the airfield
He requested soldiers from another side
He directed fire and encouraged his men
activities.explanation: Sharma directed fire, filled gunners’ magazines and encouraged his soldiers to hold their ground.

activities.prompt: Ninety soldiers face about five hundred invaders. How does Sharma most likely feel?
options: He feels certain that victory will be easy.
He feels determined to hold his ground.
He feels angry enough to stop thinking.
He feels relieved that the fighting will end.

why.He feels certain that victory will be ea: This mistake confuses a large enemy advantage with an easy fight.
This mistake mistakes determination for uncontrolled anger.
why.He feels relieved that the fighting will: This mistake reads Sharma's determination as relief.

activities.explanation: His words and actions show determination despite the heavy fire.

activities.prompt: The first attack was only a distraction. A larger attack came. Why did Sharma request air strikes?
options: The invaders could easily take the airfield.
The invaders planned to leave the valley.
The larger attack put the airfield and valley in danger.
The aircraft could not reach the target without help.

why.The invaders could easily take the airfi: This mistake confuses the invaders' wish to capture the area with an easy victory.
why.The invaders planned to leave the valley: This mistake treats the larger attack as a plan to leave the valley.
why.The aircraft could not reach the target: This mistake thinks Sharma did not need ground guidance for the aircraft.

activities.explanation: He needed air support because the larger attack threatened the airfield and valley.

activities.prompt: The defenders struggled until extra help arrived. What do “reinforcements” mean here?
options: Soldiers sent to help the defenders
Invaders sent to capture the town
Supplies sent to fill empty magazines
Panels laid out to guide aircraft

why.Invaders sent to capture the town: This mistake treats the helpers as part of the invading force.
why.Supplies sent to fill empty magazines: This mistake focuses on supplies instead of the arriving soldiers.
why.Panels laid out to guide aircraft: This mistake focuses on aircraft guidance instead of extra soldiers.

activities.explanation: Reinforcements are extra soldiers who arrive to help the defenders.

activities.prompt: “Fight with determination and courage,” his voice says. What kind of leader does this show?
options: A leader who encourages courage in difficult fighting.
A leader who asks soldiers to leave their post.
A leader who hides the strength of the enemy.
A leader who expects soldiers to stop using guns.

why.A leader who asks soldiers to leave thei: This mistake mistakes encouragement to fight for encouragement to retreat.
why.A leader who hides the strength of the e: This mistake sees confident leadership as hiding the enemy's strength.
why.A leader who expects soldiers to stop us: This mistake mistakes Sharma's encouragement for giving up the fight.

activities.explanation: His words urge courage and determination while the soldiers are under heavy fire.

activities.prompt: Sharma directs fire and fills gunners' magazines. His soldiers keep holding their ground. Why?
options: He wants the soldiers ready to keep holding their ground.
He wants the soldiers to leave the airfield and hide.
He wants the soldiers to stop firing at the invaders.
He wants the soldiers to wait until the enemy leaves.

why.He wants the soldiers to leave the airfi: This mistake treats Sharma's orders as a plan to retreat.
why.He wants the soldiers to stop firing at: This mistake thinks filling magazines means stopping the fire.
why.He wants the soldiers to wait until the: This mistake assumes the invaders planned to leave the area.

activities.explanation: These actions keep the soldiers ready and determined to hold their ground.
