lessons.title: The Last Stand and the PVC

activities.prompt: Could one soldier’s courage really change the fate of a city?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Major Sharma's Last Stand
activities.body: Major Somnath Sharma stayed with D Company when ammunition was running out. He refused an order to pull back and helped a machine-gun operator. A mortar shell killed him. His soldiers held on for over six hours, giving reinforcements time to arrive. Their resistance caused more than 300 enemy casualties. It helped save Srinagar for India. Sharma received the Param Vir Chakra after his death.
keyPoints: Sharma refused to retreat.
His soldiers held their position for over six more hours.
Their resistance helped save Srinagar for India.
activities.explanation: Major Sharma's leadership inspired his soldiers to keep fighting.

activities.prompt: D Company was running out of ammunition. Why did its leader refuse to retreat?
steps: D Company began running out of ammunition, so every round mattered.
Ordered to pull back, he vowed to fight to the last round.
He helped load the machine gun until a mortar shell killed him.
His soldiers held on, giving reinforcements time to save Srinagar.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What was happening when Sharma refused to pull back?
options: D Company had plenty of ammunition.
D Company was running out of ammunition.
D Company had abandoned its position.
D Company had received fresh ammunition.
activities.explanation: D Company began running out of ammunition.

activities.prompt: Major Somnath Sharma was awarded the ______ for conspicuous bravery.
activities.hint: This award came after his death.
activities.explanation: He received this award for conspicuous bravery, and it came after his death.

activities.prompt: Match each event with Sharma's action or its result.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an order, action or event with what followed.

activities.prompt: What did D Company do after Major Sharma died?
options: It left its position at once.
It held its position for over six more hours.
It ordered an immediate retreat.
It waited for fresh ammunition.
activities.explanation: After Sharma died, his soldiers held their position for over six more hours.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: He was ordered to pull back.
He helped the operator load the machine gun.
A mortar shell hit his position.
activities.explanation: Sharma first refused the order. He then helped the gun operator. A shell finally struck his position.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the Param Vir Chakra is true?
options: It came before his death, and he was its first recipient.
It came after his death, and he was its first recipient.
It came after his death, and he was its second recipient.
It came before his death, and he was its second recipient.
activities.explanation: Major Sharma was the first recipient, and the award came after his death.

activities.prompt: Major Sharma was ordered back but vowed to fight to the end. How did he feel?
options: He felt determined to keep fighting.
He felt relieved that the order was clear.
He felt willing to leave his soldiers.
He felt certain the danger would disappear.

why.He felt relieved that the order was clea: This mistake treats a clear order as a reason to feel relieved.
This mistake confuses duty to his soldiers with willingness to leave them.
why.He felt certain the danger would disappe: This mistake wrongly assumes that an order removes danger.

activities.explanation: Refusing the order and vowing to fight show strong determination.

activities.prompt: D Company held on for six more hours after Major Sharma died. What did this show about the soldiers?
options: They were willing to keep resisting.
They were waiting for a safer order.
They had forgotten their fallen leader.
They wanted only to protect themselves.

This mistake thinks waiting for an order means they stopped defending the position.
This mistake thinks soldiers forget their leader as soon as he dies.
This mistake confuses their duty with only personal safety.

activities.explanation: Holding their position after his death shows continued resistance.

activities.prompt: Their resistance gave reinforcements time to arrive. What might have happened if they had stopped earlier?
options: Reinforcements might have arrived less quickly.
The enemy might have had more time.
The soldiers might have reached safety.
Major Sharma might have stayed alive.

This mistake reverses cause and effect and assumes resistance helped the enemy.
This mistake wrongly assumes retreating would guarantee safety.
This mistake assumes leaving earlier would prevent the shell from killing him.

activities.explanation: Their resistance gave reinforcements time, so stopping earlier could have reduced that time.

activities.prompt: He crouched beside the machine-gun operator to help load the gun. What does this reveal about him?
options: He was willing to share danger.
He wanted to avoid the machine gun.
He preferred giving orders from far away.
He believed ammunition was unimportant.

This mistake mistakes helping the operator for avoiding danger.
why.He preferred giving orders from far away: This mistake wrongly believes a leader should stay far from danger.
This mistake ignores his urgent work with the gun ammunition.

activities.explanation: He stayed close to danger while helping the operator, so he shared it.

activities.prompt: Their resistance caused more than 300 enemy casualties and injured their leader. What does “resistance” mean here?
options: Fighting back and refusing to give up.
Leaving the position without any fight.
Waiting for reinforcements without defending the place.
Choosing another duty instead of continuing.

This mistake confuses resistance with leaving and giving up.
why.Waiting for reinforcements without defen: This mistake treats passive waiting as the same as fighting back.
why.Choosing another duty instead of continu: This mistake confuses continuing resistance with changing duties.

activities.explanation: The word describes fighting back while refusing to surrender the position.

lessons.title: Early Life and Gallantry Honours

activities.prompt: What stories and choices shaped Somnath Sharma’s brave journey?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Somnath Sharma's Early Life
activities.body: Major Somnath Sharma was born in Dadh on 31 January 1923. His family had a rich military legacy. His grandfather inspired him with brave stories from the Mahabharata. He studied at Sherwood College and trained at the Royal Military College. He joined the 8th Battalion of the 19th Hyderabad Regiment in 1942. He earned mentions in despatches for bravery. He was the first Param Vir Chakra recipient among twenty-one awardees.
keyPoints: His father, Major General Amar Nath Sharma, served the nation with distinction.
His early education was at Sherwood College, followed by military training.
He earned bravery mentions and became the first Param Vir Chakra recipient.
activities.explanation: His early life moved from family inspiration to education, training, and bravery.

activities.prompt: A child asks why Major Somnath Sharma followed a brave military path.
steps: His father served the nation with distinction, giving him a brave example.
His grandfather's Mahabharata stories inspired him to admire courage.
His rigorous training at Sandhurst prepared him for army service.
So family example and training helped him earn gallantry honours.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where was Major Somnath Sharma born?
options: Dadh
Nainital
Sandhurst
Hyderabad
activities.explanation: He was born in Dadh, not Nainital or Sandhurst.

activities.prompt: He received his early education at Sherwood College in Nainital.
activities.explanation: Sherwood College in Nainital was the place of his early education.

activities.prompt: Match each stage with the correct place or unit.
activities.explanation: The lesson links each stage to the correct college or regiment.

activities.prompt: He was commissioned into the 8th Battalion of the 19th Hyderabad Regiment in ______.
activities.hint: Choose the year of his commissioning.
activities.explanation: He was commissioned into that regiment in 1942.

activities.prompt: Which award is India's highest military award for conspicuous bravery?
options: Param Vir Chakra
Sherwood College
Royal Military College
8th Battalion of the 19th Hyderabad Regiment
activities.explanation: The Param Vir Chakra is India's highest military award for conspicuous bravery.

activities.prompt: Put these stages of Somnath Sharma's early military life in order.
items: Rigorous training at the Royal Military College
Commissioning into the 8th Battalion of the 19th Hyderabad Regiment
activities.explanation: He received early education first, training next, and commissioning later.

activities.prompt: Major Somnath Sharma had a rich military family legacy. His father served with distinction. His grandfather inspired him with Mahabharata stories. How did this background affect him?
options: They made him want to serve bravely.
They made him dislike soldiers altogether.
They made him forget his father's service.
They made him choose only school life.

why.They made him dislike soldiers altogethe: This mistake thinks family courage made him dislike soldiers.
why.They made him forget his father's servic: This mistake forgets his father's service influenced him.
This mistake assumes the stories pushed him toward school only.

activities.explanation: This is right because brave stories and example inspired his service.

activities.prompt: He received rigorous training at the Royal Military College in Sandhurst. What does 'rigorous' suggest about this training?
options: It was hard and carefully demanding.
It was easy and needed little effort.
It was short and mostly playful.
It was gentle and had no rules.

This mistake treats rigorous training as easy work.
This mistake thinks rigorous means short and playful.
This mistake believes rigorous training has no rules.

activities.explanation: Rigorous means hard and demanding, so this option fits.

activities.prompt: Major Somnath Sharma was commissioned into the 8th Battalion of the 19th Hyderabad Regiment in 1942. What does 'commissioned' mean here?
options: He was given an army post.
He was asked to leave the army.
He was sent to train at home.
He was given a school award.

This mistake thinks commissioned means leaving the army.
This mistake confuses commissioning with home training.
This mistake confuses commissioning with a school prize.

activities.explanation: Commissioned means he was given an army post.

activities.prompt: Among twenty-one PVC awardees, Major Somnath Sharma was the first recipient. Captain Vikram Batra was the last recipient. What does this pair of facts show?
options: They stood at opposite ends of the awardees' list.
They received the same award at the same time.
Only one of them received a military award.
They both refused the award's bravery honour.

why.They received the same award at the same: This mistake thinks first and last mean the same time.
why.Only one of them received a military awa: This mistake believes only one person received the award.
why.They both refused the award's bravery ho: This mistake thinks both rejected the bravery honour.

activities.explanation: First and last place the men at opposite ends of the list.

activities.context: Kashmir Valley became the setting for an extraordinary battle. Major Somnath Sharma led 90 men on a mission to protect Srinagar airport. Their action stopped about 500 infiltrators from taking Srinagar. The invaders hoped to capture the city and strike newly independent India. When the battle ended, echoes of courage inspired later generations, keeping the legacy of Somnath Sharma’s courage and devotion alive.
activities.prompt: If the invaders had captured Srinagar before the 90 men could stop them, what would likely have happened next?
options: Newly independent India would face an attack from the invaders.
The defenders’ mission would succeed without any further danger.
The invaders would decide that capturing Srinagar was no longer useful.
Later generations would remember the mission as ordinary rather than courageous.

why.The defenders’ mission would succeed wit: Capturing the city would have endangered the defenders’ mission.
why.The invaders would decide that capturing: The invaders’ aim was to capture the city, not give it up.
why.Later generations would remember the mis: The mission was remembered because of its courage and sacrifice.

activities.explanation: The invaders wanted to capture Srinagar and strike newly independent India.

activities.context: Kashmir Valley became the setting for an extraordinary battle. Major Somnath Sharma led 90 men on a mission to protect Srinagar airport. Their action stopped about 500 infiltrators from taking Srinagar. The invaders hoped to capture the city and strike newly independent India. When the battle ended, echoes of courage inspired later generations, keeping the legacy of Somnath Sharma’s courage and devotion alive.
activities.prompt: Why did the action of the 90 men have lasting importance?
options: It showed that courage and sacrifice can defend a nation and encourage later generations.
The defenders’ success depended mainly on the larger number of infiltrators.
Protecting the airport mattered more than the courage shown by the 90 men.
Later generations were inspired because the invaders reached Srinagar.

why.The defenders’ success depended mainly o: The larger number of invaders did not cancel the courage of the defenders.
why.Protecting the airport mattered more tha: The mission’s importance came from both its purpose and the courage behind it.
why.Later generations were inspired because: The invaders were stopped, so they did not capture Srinagar.

activities.explanation: Their courage and sacrifice inspired generations of people.

activities.context: Kashmir Valley became the setting for an extraordinary battle. Major Somnath Sharma led 90 men on a mission to protect Srinagar airport. Their action stopped about 500 infiltrators from taking Srinagar. The invaders hoped to capture the city and strike newly independent India. When the battle ended, echoes of courage inspired later generations, keeping the legacy of Somnath Sharma’s courage and devotion alive.
activities.prompt: After the first battle, another group of invaders tries to enter Srinagar. What should the 90 men do?
options: Continue guarding the airport and prevent the newcomers from taking Srinagar.
Help the newcomers enter the city so they can use the airport.
Leave the airport undefended because the first group of about 500 was stopped.
Follow the newcomers toward newly independent India.

why.Help the newcomers enter the city so the: Helping the newcomers would weaken the mission they had completed.
why.Leave the airport undefended because the: Stopping one group did not remove the need to protect the airport.
why.Follow the newcomers toward newly indepe: Following the newcomers would help the invaders instead of defending Srinagar.

activities.explanation: Their mission was to protect Srinagar airport and prevent the invaders from taking the city.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Major Somnath Sharma was India’s first Param Vir Chakra recipient.
Reason (R): His name has been fixed in the annals of history.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but being remembered in history does not explain why he received the honour.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The 90 men stopped about 500 infiltrators from taking Srinagar.
Reason (R): They were carrying out a mission to protect Srinagar airport under Major Somnath Sharma.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the mission to protect the airport explains why they acted to stop the infiltrators.

activities.prompt: How did Major Somnath Sharma’s national honour and his mission in Kashmir Valley both show courage and sacrifice?
activities.answer: Major Somnath Sharma’s national honour and his mission reflected the same courage and sacrifice in different ways. As India’s first Param Vir Chakra recipient, he became a lasting figure in the annals of history. In Kashmir Valley, he led 90 men to protect Srinagar airport, and their stand stopped about 500 infiltrators from taking Srinagar. The invaders aimed to capture the city and strike newly independent India. By facing that danger, Somnath Sharma and his men showed courage and devotion to the nation, while their sacrifice became an example for later generations.
points: Somnath Sharma was India’s first Param Vir Chakra recipient.
He led 90 men on a mission in Kashmir Valley.
The mission protected Srinagar airport and stopped about 500 infiltrators.
Their courage and sacrifice inspired later generations.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In August 1947, events leading to the Battle of Badgam began. Pakistan planned Operation Gulmarg to annex the Kashmir Valley, despite agreeing with Hari Singh not to attack Jammu and Kashmir. Around 1000 invaders were trained and equipped and knew the local terrain well. Their plan was to cause a revolt, capture territory and control important passes, peaks and rivers. Operation Gulmarg began on 22 October. Indian troops reached Srinagar by air because the land route was badly damaged.
activities.prompt: If the invaders had not known the local terrain, what would most likely have happened?
options: They would have found movement across the area more difficult.
They would have made faster progress across the area.
They would have found the local terrain easier to use.
They would have identified every route without training or equipment.

why.They would have made faster progress acr: Ignoring the terrain would not make their movement faster.
why.They would have found the local terrain: Lack of local knowledge would not make the terrain easier to use.
why.They would have identified every route w: Training, equipment and local knowledge could not simply be replaced by ignorance.

activities.explanation: Their knowledge of the terrain would normally help them move through the area.

activities.context: In August 1947, events leading to the Battle of Badgam began. Pakistan planned Operation Gulmarg to annex the Kashmir Valley, despite agreeing with Hari Singh not to attack Jammu and Kashmir. Around 1000 invaders were trained and equipped and knew the local terrain well. Their plan was to cause a revolt, capture territory and control important passes, peaks and rivers. Operation Gulmarg began on 22 October. Indian troops reached Srinagar by air because the land route was badly damaged.
activities.prompt: Why were the troops taken to Srinagar by air rather than by the land route?
options: The overland journey was difficult because the route had been damaged.
The air journey was chosen simply because the troops preferred it.
The troops were sent by air to avoid meeting the invaders.
Srinagar could not be reached by land under any conditions.

why.The air journey was chosen simply becaus: A preference for air travel does not explain the official decision.
why.The troops were sent by air to avoid mee: There is no stated reason to believe that they avoided the invaders because of the journey.
why.Srinagar could not be reached by land un: The land route was badly damaged, but this does not mean land travel was impossible in every condition.

activities.explanation: Damage to the land route was the stated reason for using air transport.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Pakistan launched Operation Gulmarg on 22 October 1947.
Reason (R): The operation was intended to annex the Kashmir Valley.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains the purpose of the operation but not why it began on 22 October 1947.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Pakistani invaders had advantages when they entered the Kashmir Valley.
activities.answer: The Pakistani invaders had important advantages. Around 1000 of them were trained and equipped, so they were ready to carry out the operation. They also knew the mountain passes and local terrain well, which helped them move through the area and use its features. Their plan was to cause a revolt, overthrow the government and capture the territory. Capturing Kashmir would also give them control of important passes, peaks and rivers, strengthening the value of their plan.
points: Around 1000 invaders were trained and equipped.
They knew the mountain passes and local terrain well.
Their plan included causing a revolt and overthrowing the government.
Capturing Kashmir would give them control of important passes, peaks and rivers.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On 3 November, Major Somnath Sharma was with D Company, which left the patrol last with 90 soldiers. His left hand was in plaster, but he insisted on joining his company and refused to let his men enter action without him. Badgam was less than 5 kilometres from Srinagar airport; controlling it would protect Indian troops and allow supplies to arrive. The enemy entered in small groups to avoid detection, but its first attack met stiff resistance.
activities.prompt: What should Major Somnath Sharma do when his company enters action?
options: Remain with his company and lead the response
Keep away from action until his hand had healed
Allow his men to begin fighting before he reached them
Leave the patrol under another officer at the first sign of danger

why.Keep away from action until his hand had: This ignores his insistence on joining despite his injury.
why.Allow his men to begin fighting before h: This contradicts his refusal to let his men act without him.
why.Leave the patrol under another officer a: This also contradicts his refusal to leave his men without him.

activities.explanation: This follows his decision to remain with his company.

The enemy would have found it easier to avoid the patrols
The enemy would have needed more soldiers to remain unnoticed

why.The enemy would have needed more soldier: Staying unnoticed would not require more soldiers in a large group.
why.The enemy would have been able to enter: The enemy still met stiff resistance from Major Somnath and his men.

activities.explanation: A large group would be easier to detect than small groups.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Major Somnath Sharma showed strong commitment to his men and country.
Reason (R): He refused to let his men enter action without him.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: His refusal directly shows that he was determined to stand with his men and share responsibility for the country’s defence.

activities.prompt:

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

activities.explanation: The assertion is false because control would also protect Indian troops, while the reason given about air supplies is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why Major Somnath Sharma’s decision to join his company showed strong commitment.
activities.answer: Major Somnath Sharma showed commitment by choosing to be with his company even though his left hand was in plaster. He refused to let his men enter action without him, so he wanted to share the responsibility of facing the enemy with the soldiers under his command. His words and actions showed that his duty did not end because he was injured. When the enemy’s first attack came, Major Somnath and his men met it with stiff resistance. This shows that he was determined to lead his men in action and remain committed to his men and country.
points: He insisted on joining despite his injured hand
He refused to let his men enter action without him
He shared responsibility with the soldiers
His conduct reflected commitment to his men and country

activities.context: Major Somnath Sharma saw that the first attack was a distraction. A larger attack came from another side, so his 90 soldiers faced about 500 invaders, almost seven to one. options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

lessons.title: Before the Story: Words and Cases

activities.prompt: What do an anagram, a subject line, and a pencil case have in common?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words to Know
activities.body: Before reading, learn these useful word groups. An anagram rearranges the same letters to make a new word or phrase. A legal case can be taken up in court. In a formal letter, the subject is written in title case. An encyclopedia contains facts. Encyclopedia Brown lives in Idaville, in the USA. His father is the Chief of Police. His family usually discusses cases at the dining table.
keyPoints: An anagram uses the same letters in a different order.
A legal case can be taken up in court.
An encyclopedia is filled with facts.
Encyclopedia Brown's father is the Chief of Police.
activities.explanation: These clues prepare you for the words, people and cases in the story.

activities.prompt: Encyclopedia is solving a difficult case while his father is still eating. Who can finish first?
steps: His father is the Chief of Police, so cases are closely connected with him.
The family usually discusses cases at the dining table, so the case comes up during dinner.
Encyclopedia can solve a difficult case before his father finishes dinner.
Therefore, Encyclopedia finishes first while his father is still eating.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does an anagram do?
options: Uses new letters in the same order
Uses the same letters in a new order
Changes every letter in a word
Adds different letters to a word
activities.explanation: An anagram keeps all the same letters. It changes their order to make a new word or phrase.

activities.prompt: An encyclopedia is a book or set of books filled with ______.
activities.hint: Think of a book full of information.
activities.explanation: An encyclopedia is a book or set of books filled with facts.

activities.prompt: Match each word or group with its meaning.
pairs: Same letters in a different order
Can be taken up in court
A book or set of books filled with facts
activities.explanation: Each match gives a definition from the lesson. Read each pair once more to check it.

activities.prompt: Who calls Encyclopedia 'Leroy'?
options: His parents only
His teachers only
His neighbours only
His parents and teachers
activities.explanation: Only Encyclopedia's parents and teachers call him Leroy. Everyone else calls him Encyclopedia.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for making an anagram in order.
items: Put the letters in a different order.
Make a new word or phrase.
activities.explanation: An anagram keeps the same letters. Their order changes to make a new word or phrase.

activities.prompt: While the family discusses cases at the dining table, who is the Chief of Police?
options: Encyclopedia Brown's father
Encyclopedia Brown
His dinner guest
His neighbour
activities.explanation: Encyclopedia's father is the Chief of Police. Encyclopedia can solve a difficult case before his father finishes dinner.

activities.prompt: A child rearranges “listen” to make “silent.” What makes the new word an anagram?
options: It uses the same letters in a different order.
It uses the same sounds in a different order.
It uses one new letter and keeps all the others.
It gives each old letter a different sound.

why.It uses the same sounds in a different o: This confuses changing letter order with changing sounds.
why.It uses one new letter and keeps all the: This wrongly suggests that an anagram adds a letter.
why.It gives each old letter a different sou: This wrongly suggests that anagrammed letters change sound.

activities.explanation: Correct: it keeps every letter but changes their order.

options: It was a legal case that could be dealt with in court.
It was a pencil case shared by the two neighbours.
It was an encyclopedia about arguments between two neighbours.
It was an anagram showing the names of two neighbours.

why.It was a pencil case shared by the two n: This mistakes a court dispute for a container.
why.It was an encyclopedia about arguments b: This mistakes a reference book for something taken to court.
why.It was an anagram showing the names of t: This mistakes a disagreement for a rearrangement of letters.

activities.explanation: Correct: a legal case can be taken up in court.

options: Only parents and teachers call him Leroy; everyone else says Encyclopedia.
His father calls him Encyclopedia because Leroy belongs to the Chief of Police.
His friends call him Encyclopedia because Leroy belongs to his teacher.
Both names belong to everyone living with him in Idaville.

why.His father calls him Encyclopedia becaus: This wrongly connects Leroy with the father’s police role.
why.His friends call him Encyclopedia becaus: This wrongly gives Leroy only to the teacher.
why.Both names belong to everyone living wit: This wrongly treats Leroy as a name for the whole town.

activities.explanation: Correct: only parents and teachers call him Leroy.

activities.prompt: At dinner, Encyclopedia’s father is the Chief of Police. Encyclopedia solves a difficult case. His father has not finished eating. What does this show?

He needs his father to finish dinner first.
He can solve only easy cases at the table.
He cannot work while the family discusses cases.

why.He needs his father to finish dinner fir: This reverses the timing because his father eats later.
why.He can solve only easy cases at the tabl: This wrongly limits his solved case to an easy one.
why.He cannot work while the family discusse: This wrongly makes family discussion block his solving.

activities.explanation: Correct: solving first shows that he works quickly on difficult cases.

activities.prompt: A reader opens a book filled with facts. Why would the reader choose this book?

To keep pencils safe while reading many facts.
To send a disagreement to be heard by a court.
To rearrange letters into a new word or phrase.

why.To send a disagreement to be heard by a: This mistakes the book for a legal case.
why.To rearrange letters into a new word or: This mistakes the book for an anagram.

activities.explanation: Correct: an encyclopedia is filled with facts.

activities.title: The robbery and investigation
activities.body: Tim Nolan died the day before the family dinner, after a stroke. Two masked men robbed the Diamond Mart, escaping with jewellery worth a million dollars. Nolan was questioned but not arrested. No proof was found against him or Daniel Davenport. Police searched Nolan’s house, but found no jewellery. No trace of the stolen jewellery was ever found. Nolan left his nursery and everything else to Davenport.

Angry and playful because the dinner went badly.

why.Happy and relieved because the dinner wa: This mistakes a family death for a happy, welcome change.
why.Excited and hopeful because the dinner w: This mistakes an unhappy loss for a happy finish to the dinner.
why.Angry and playful because the dinner wen: This mistakes sadness for anger and play without support.

activities.explanation: The death before the dinner would bring sadness and disappointment.

activities.prompt: Two masked men robbed the Diamond Mart. Why did they cover their faces?
options: They wanted to keep people from identifying them.
They wanted to make the robbery look like an accident.
They wanted to keep the jewellery safe from harm.
They wanted to warn people before taking the jewellery.

why.They wanted to make the robbery look lik: This confuses hiding identity with disguising what happened.
why.They wanted to keep the jewellery safe f: This confuses taking jewellery with protecting it from harm.
why.They wanted to warn people before taking: This confuses hiding identity with announcing the crime.

activities.explanation: Masks hide identity, so the robbers could avoid being recognized.

activities.prompt: The stolen jewellery was worth a million dollars. No trace was ever found. If police found it, what would it show?
options: It would prove that Nolan had planned the robbery.
It could show who had the stolen goods.
It would prove that Davenport had taken every piece.
It would show that the clerk knew both robbers.

why.It would prove that Nolan had planned th: Finding the goods would not prove that Nolan planned the robbery.
why.It would prove that Davenport had taken: Finding the goods would not prove that Davenport took every piece.
why.It would show that the clerk knew both r: Finding the goods would not reveal what the clerk knew.

activities.explanation: Finding the goods could show who had them and support the case.

activities.prompt: Nolan was questioned about the robbery but was not arrested. A clerk refused to give evidence against him. How should we treat that refusal?
options: It shows a weak case, not proof of guilt.
It proves that Nolan ordered the clerk to stay silent.
It proves that the clerk helped plan the robbery.
It shows that police had already proved the theft.

why.It proves that Nolan ordered the clerk t: This treats a missing statement as proof of a secret order.
why.It proves that the clerk helped plan the: This treats a missing statement as proof of planning.
why.It shows that police had already proved: This treats a missing statement as proof that police knew everything.

activities.explanation: The refusal gives no support and cannot prove Nolan guilty.

activities.prompt: Police searched Nolan's house thoroughly but found no jewellery. How did this affect the case?
options: It proved that Nolan had planned the robbery.
It showed that the clerk had hidden the jewellery.
It left the police without evidence from the house.
It meant the police had already found the real robbers.

why.It proved that Nolan had planned the rob: This confuses an empty search with proof of planning.
why.It showed that the clerk had hidden the: This confuses an empty search with proof about the clerk.
why.It meant the police had already found th: This assumes a failed search means the real robbers were found.

activities.explanation: The search found no jewellery, so it gave the police no evidence.

activities.prompt: No proof was found against Davenport. He had not been seen since the robbery. Nolan died after a stroke. He left everything to Davenport. What is a fair conclusion?
options: Davenport's inheritance proved that he planned the robbery.
Davenport's absence proved that he was completely innocent.
Davenport's inheritance meant the police stopped investigating.
Davenport gained property while his role stayed uncertain.

why.Davenport's inheritance proved that he p: This mistakes an inheritance for proof of planning.
why.Davenport's absence proved that he was c: This mistakes an absence for proof of innocence.
why.Davenport's inheritance meant the police: This wrongly treats inheritance as a reason the police must stop.

activities.explanation: He inherited property, but his absence left his role uncertain.

lessons.title: The Strange Calendar Message

activities.prompt: Could a strange calendar message reveal where someone had hidden something?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Strange Clue
activities.body: The will itself was not strange, but a desk calendar sheet was fixed to it. Chief Brown copied Nolan’s writing from the sheet. The writing included Davenport’s name, address, and four mysterious words: Nom Utes Sweden Hurts. Mrs Brown understood that these words could reveal the hiding place. Chief Brown now knew where to find Davenport.
keyPoints: A calendar sheet was fixed to the will.
The writing included Davenport’s name and address.
The four words could reveal the hiding place.
activities.explanation: The strange part was the attached sheet, not the will.

activities.prompt: Why could four strange words on a calendar sheet help find Davenport?
steps: They studied the calendar sheet, because the will itself was not strange.
Chief Brown copied Nolan’s writing, including Davenport’s address and four words.
Nolan’s words may explain the hiding place because he had changed it.
Mrs Brown understood the clue, so Chief Brown knew Davenport’s location.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the copied writing include?
options: Davenport’s name and address
a young fir tree
the calendar sheet
the hiding place
activities.explanation: The writing included Davenport’s name and address.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its fact from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a clue with what happened in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Chief Brown had copied Nolan’s ______ from the calendar sheet.
activities.hint: It included Davenport’s name and address.
activities.explanation: Chief Brown copied Nolan’s writing from the sheet.

activities.prompt: What did Mrs Brown understand about the four mysterious words?
options: They could reveal the hiding place
They could reveal the robbery plan
They could reveal Nolan’s address
They could reveal the calendar date
activities.explanation: Mrs Brown understood that the words could reveal the hiding place.

activities.prompt: What did Encyclopedia think Nolan had recently changed?
options: the hiding place
the calendar sheet
his writing
Davenport’s address
activities.explanation: Encyclopedia thought Nolan had recently changed the hiding place.

activities.prompt: Put the four mysterious words in their written order.
activities.explanation: The words were written in this order: Nom Utes Sweden Hurts.

activities.prompt: Mrs Brown understood the four mysterious words. Chief Brown knew where to find Davenport. How did Chief Brown feel?
options: He felt worried the words were useless.
He felt afraid the calendar sheet would vanish.
He felt certain about finding Davenport.
He felt angry that Nolan had hidden the address.

He may have thought the four words had no useful meaning.
why.He felt afraid the calendar sheet would: He may have feared the evidence would suddenly disappear.
why.He felt angry that Nolan had hidden the: He may have blamed Nolan for hiding Davenport’s address.

activities.explanation: Knowing Davenport’s location made him feel certain.

activities.prompt: Encyclopedia asked about a young fir tree in Nolan’s nursery. What might his question show?
options: He thought the tree held the stolen jewellery.
He thought the tree was planted after the robbery.
He thought Davenport lived near that tree.
He thought the tree might connect with Nolan’s clue.

why.He thought the tree held the stolen jewe: He may have confused a clue with the stolen jewellery.
why.He thought the tree was planted after th: He may have thought the tree was planted after the robbery.
why.He thought Davenport lived near that tre: He may have treated the tree as proof that Davenport lived nearby.

activities.explanation: Asking about the tree suggests Nolan’s clue might involve it.

activities.prompt: A sheet from the desk calendar was fixed to the will. Nolan’s writing included Davenport’s address. Why was the sheet important?
options: It showed where Nolan worked each day.
It held clues that pointed to Davenport’s hiding place.
It listed the people who owned the jewellery.
It explained why the will had been written.

He may have thought it showed Nolan’s daily work.
why.It listed the people who owned the jewel: He may have confused the calendar with a list of owners.
why.It explained why the will had been writt: He may have thought the will had no clear purpose.

activities.explanation: The writing on it pointed toward Davenport’s hiding place.

activities.prompt: Nolan may have written the words while dying. Mrs Brown suggested that Nolan had tried to telephone Davenport. What did she think the words could show?
options: That Nolan tried to send Davenport a message.
That Nolan wanted to meet Davenport again.
That Davenport had planned the jewellery robbery.
That Nolan had copied the calendar sheet.

why.That Nolan wanted to meet Davenport agai: She may have thought Nolan only wanted another meeting.
why.That Davenport had planned the jewellery: She may have blamed Davenport for planning the robbery.
why.That Nolan had copied the calendar sheet: She may have thought Nolan merely copied some words.

activities.explanation: She thought the words might record a telephone message.

lessons.title: Solving the Fifth Word Code

activities.prompt: Can you solve the secret fifth word?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Calendar Code
activities.body: Nolan wrote a four-word code for Davenport. A calendar sheet was the key. The words stood for four days of the week. He removed the letters d-a-y from those days. Nom meant Monday, while Utes meant Tuesday. Sweden meant Wednesday, and Hurts meant Thursday. The missing fifth word was Fir, meaning Friday.
keyPoints: The calendar sheet served as the code key.
The code words represented four days.
Fir was the missing fifth word for Friday.
activities.explanation: The day names and code words work together as a calendar key.

activities.prompt: How can you find the missing fifth word in a weekday code?
steps: Use the calendar sheet, because it is the key to the code.
Match Nom, Utes, Sweden, and Hurts to their four days.
Notice that Nolan removed the letters d-a-y from each day name.
Find Fir as the missing fifth word, so it represents Friday.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What served as the key to the code?
options: A calendar sheet
A treasure guide
A chessboard
A market list
activities.explanation: The calendar sheet served as the key to the code.

activities.prompt: Nom represented the day ______.
activities.hint: Choose the day named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Nom was the code word for Monday.

activities.prompt: Match each code word to its day.
activities.explanation: Each code word matches the day it represented.

activities.prompt: Put these days in order.
activities.explanation: These days appear in the order Monday to Friday.

activities.prompt: What did the missing fifth word, Fir, mean?
options: Monday
Tuesday
Wednesday
Friday
activities.explanation: Fir was the missing fifth word, and it meant Friday.

activities.prompt: What was growing from the earth in the jug?
options: A young fir tree
The calendar sheet
The four-word code
The word Fir
activities.explanation: A young fir tree grew from the earth in the twenty-gallon jug. The jewellery was also hidden there.

activities.prompt: Nom means Monday. Utes means Tuesday. Fir follows the same code. Which day does it mean?
options: It means Monday.
It means Tuesday.
It means Thursday.
It means Friday.

Correct: Fir is the missing fifth word, and it means Friday.
Wrong: Monday is already represented by Nom.
Wrong: Tuesday is already represented by Utes.

activities.explanation: Wrong: Thursday is already represented by Hurts.

activities.prompt: Utes means Tuesday. What change best explains this shorter word?
options: The letters d, a and y were removed.
The first and last day letters were removed.
The three middle day letters were removed.
The whole day word was written backwards.

why.The first and last day letters were remo: Wrong: This choice wrongly removes only the outside letters.
why.The three middle day letters were remove: Wrong: This choice wrongly focuses on the middle letters.
why.The whole day word was written backwards: Wrong: This choice ignores the removal of the letters d-a-y.

activities.explanation: Correct: Nolan removed the letters d-a-y from the days of the week.

activities.prompt: The code words stand for four days. The calendar sheet is missing. What problem will this cause?
options: The code cannot be checked against its key.
The five code words will become days again.
The hidden young tree will grow more quickly.
The earlier prediction will change by itself.

why.The five code words will become days aga: Wrong: Missing the key does not turn the code words into day names.
why.The hidden young tree will grow more qui: Wrong: Missing the sheet does not change the tree's growth.
why.The earlier prediction will change by it: Wrong: Missing the sheet does not change an earlier prediction.

activities.explanation: Correct: The calendar sheet was the key for checking the code.

activities.prompt: A prediction was made. The discovery later matched it. How did Encyclopedia likely feel?
options: Surprised that the prediction was right.
Afraid that the prediction was wrong.
Angry that the prediction was ignored.
Glad that the prediction stayed unknown.

Wrong: The discovery matched, so the prediction was not wrong.
Wrong: Nothing says that the prediction was ignored.
Wrong: The discovery did not stay unknown.

activities.explanation: Correct: A discovery matching an earlier prediction can cause surprise.

activities.prompt: A child says, “Friday is the best day.” What kind of statement is this?
options: It is a fact because Friday is a real day.
It is an opinion because people may vary.
It is a fact because Friday is in the code.
It is an opinion because Friday is the last word.

why.It is a fact because Friday is a real da: Correct: “Best” shows a judgement, and such judgements may vary.
why.It is a fact because Friday is in the co: Wrong: A day's place in the code does not prove this judgement.
why.It is an opinion because Friday is the l: Wrong: Being the last code word does not make a judgement a fact.

activities.explanation: Wrong: Naming a real day does not make a claim about it true.

activities.prompt: A fir tree grows inside earth in a jug. Why can this statement be checked?
options: Because it describes something that can be proved.
Because it expresses a personal feeling.
Because it gives a belief about Friday.
Because it predicts what the next day will be.

Wrong: The statement describes a tree, not a personal feeling.
Wrong: The statement is about the tree, not a belief about Friday.
why.Because it predicts what the next day wi: Wrong: The statement reports a discovery, not a prediction about a day.

activities.explanation: Correct: The tree and its place can be checked, so the statement is a fact.

lessons.title: Leroy’s Character and the Clues

activities.prompt: What surprising clues reveal what Leroy is really like?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Character and Clues
activities.body: Leroy is known by his real name, Leroy, but everyone gives him a nickname he cannot change. He is humble because he does not want to seem different. His strong memory and cleverness help him solve cases. Other clues show that Chief Brown and Mrs Brown could not understand or decode the message. The story also traces how Nolan and Davenport became friends, and when Davenport moved in with Nolan.
keyPoints: Leroy’s real name is Leroy, and others give him a nickname.
He is humble, has a strong memory, and is clever.
Friendship and shared interests form important clues.
activities.explanation: These details help you notice how words and actions reveal character.

activities.prompt: How can Leroy be clever while staying humble around other boys?
steps: He never forgets a fact after reading it because his memory is strong.
He solves a case after one question because he is clever.
He does not want to seem different from other boys because he is humble.
Therefore, Leroy is both clever and humble at the same time.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Leroy’s Real Name
activities.prompt: What name do Leroy’s parents and teachers use?
options: Leroy
A chosen nickname
A secret title
A different name
activities.explanation: His parents and teachers know him by his real name, Leroy.

activities.title: The Nickname
activities.prompt: Leroy can change the nickname given to him by everyone else.
activities.explanation: Everyone else gives him the nickname, and Leroy cannot change it.

activities.title: Leroy’s Memory
activities.prompt: Leroy never forgets a ______ that he has read.
activities.hint: Think about what he remembers after reading.
activities.explanation: Leroy never forgets a fact that he has read.

activities.title: Nolan and Davenport’s Story
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: They met in prison in South Carolina.
They became friendly because they shared interests.
Davenport went to live with Nolan one week before the robbery.
activities.explanation: They met first, became friendly, and then Davenport moved in.

activities.title: The Four Words
activities.prompt: Chief Brown understood the four words in the notebook.
activities.explanation: Chief Brown could not understand the four words, so he returned the notebook.

activities.title: A Correct Picture of Leroy
activities.prompt: Which option gives a correct picture of Leroy?
options: He is proud, forgetful, and unable to solve cases.
He is humble, forgetful, and unable to solve cases.
He is humble, careful with facts, and clever at solving cases.
He is clever, wants to seem different, and changes nicknames.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows Leroy as humble, careful with facts, and clever at solving cases.

activities.prompt: Leroy does not want to seem different from other boys. How might he choose to act at school?
options: He tries to look cleverer than them.
He tries to seem more different.
He tries to look like the other boys.
He tries to show every fact.

This mistakes his wish to belong for a wish to impress.
This reverses his wish not to seem different.
This mistakes remembering facts for a wish to show off.

activities.explanation: He wants not to seem different from other boys.

activities.prompt: A case is hard to solve. Leroy asks one question and solves it. What does this show?
options: He has trouble starting any case.
He has a clever way of solving cases.
He needs many questions before solving.
He depends on others to solve it.

This mistakes one successful case for a general problem.
He actually needs only one question.
His success shows skill, not dependence on others.

activities.explanation: Solving a case after one question shows that he is clever.

activities.prompt: Leroy has read a fact. Much later, someone asks him about it. What will he likely do?
options: He will give a different fact.
He will say that he forgot it.
He will ask about the case instead.
He will give the fact accurately.

This confuses remembering a fact with changing it.
This ignores that he never forgets what he reads.
This mixes his memory with his skill at solving cases.

activities.explanation: He never forgets a fact that he has read.

activities.prompt: Leroy’s parents and teachers call him Leroy. Everyone else gives him a nickname. He cannot change it. How might he respond?
options: He may accept it because he cannot change it.
He may think his real name has vanished.
He may expect the nickname to disappear.
He may want everyone to use another name.

His parents and teachers still know him as Leroy.
The nickname from everyone else cannot be changed.
why.He may want everyone to use another name: This mistakes his lack of control for a wish to control them.

activities.explanation: Since he cannot change it, accepting it is sensible.

activities.prompt: Chief Brown could not understand the four words. Mrs Brown also could not decode the message. What can we work out about the message?
options: The message was easy for Chief Brown.
The notebook did not contain a message.
The message was hard for both of them.
The message was meant only for Mrs Brown.

He could not understand the four words.
He passed a notebook that contained the message.
why.The message was meant only for Mrs Brown: Neither clue shows that it was meant only for Mrs Brown.

activities.explanation: Both Chief Brown and Mrs Brown failed to decode it.

activities.prompt: Nolan and Davenport met in prison in South Carolina. They shared interests and became friendly. Davenport moved in with Nolan one week before the robbery. What can we infer?
options: They first met during the robbery.
They were friendly before the robbery.
They became friendly after the robbery.
They had no shared interests at all.

This mistakes the robbery for the time they first met.
This reverses the order of their friendship and the robbery.
They became friendly because they shared interests.

activities.explanation: Davenport moved in with Nolan before the robbery.

lessons.title: Language, Observation and Writing

activities.prompt: How can we notice, describe, and write about what we discover?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Language, Observation and Writing
activities.body: You practise useful phrases. “Turned up” describes important evidence appearing. “Put on” describes wearing a special coat. “Figure out” means understanding a big mistake. Reported speech can change person, tense, place and time. Questions become statements, and question words follow reporting verbs. Good observers slow down, use their senses, and take notes or sketches. Reports describe past events in sequence. A falling tone is usually used for an imperative giving an instruction.
keyPoints: “Turned up” means important evidence appeared.
“Put on” means wearing a special coat.
“Figure out” means understanding a big mistake.
Reported speech can change person, tense, place and time.
Questions become statements in reported speech.
Question words follow reporting verbs.
Observers should slow down and use their senses.
Notes and sketches can strengthen understanding.
Reports present past events in sequence.
Imperative sentences usually have a falling tone.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you report, observe and write clearly.

activities.prompt: How can you make a clear report when important evidence turns up?
steps: First, slow down and use your senses, because careful observers learn more.
Next, take notes or make sketches, because they can strengthen your understanding.
Change person and tense if needed, because reported speech can change them.
Then report what happened in order, because the event is already over.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does “turned up” describe in the lesson?
options: Important evidence appearing
Evidence staying hidden
A special coat being worn
A big mistake understood
activities.explanation: “Turned up” is used when important evidence appears.

activities.prompt: Match each phrase with its use in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each phrase matches the action described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: In reported Wh-questions, the question word comes ______ after the reporting verb.
activities.hint: Think about the exact position.
activities.explanation: The question word comes immediately after the reporting verb.

activities.prompt: Which action helps a good observer?
options: Use their senses
Use only their eyes
Skip careful looking
Rush past details
activities.explanation: Using all your senses can help you learn more.

activities.prompt: An interrogative sentence becomes a declarative sentence in reported speech.
activities.explanation: An interrogative is a question. A declarative is a statement.

activities.prompt: When is a report written?
options: After the event
Before it starts
While it begins
Before it is planned
activities.explanation: A report is written about an event that has already happened.

activities.prompt: Important evidence has turned up. What should a careful observer do?
options: Take time, use all senses, and make notes.
Guess fast, use no senses, and make no notes.
Skip careful looking and trust a quick guess.
Change the evidence and avoid taking notes.

why.Guess fast, use no senses, and make no n: This wrongly treats quick guessing as careful observation.
why.Skip careful looking and trust a quick g: This wrongly rejects slow, careful looking.
why.Change the evidence and avoid taking not: This wrongly suggests changing evidence instead of recording it.

activities.explanation: This follows careful observing, using senses, and making notes.

activities.prompt: A friend asks, “Where did you see the evidence?” Which report is correct?
options: You asked where I saw the evidence.
You asked me where did I see the evidence.
You asked where did I see the evidence.
You asked the evidence where I saw it.

why.You asked me where did I see the evidenc: This wrongly keeps the direct question form after “asked”.
This wrongly keeps “did” inside the reported question.
This wrongly moves the question word away from the reporting verb.

activities.explanation: It changes person and tense, and places “where” after “asked”.

activities.prompt: The teacher says, “Close the window!” The sentence has a falling tone. What does it show?
options: It is a firm command, not a question.
It is an uncertain question, not a command.
It is a friendly wish, not a command.
It is a report, not a spoken command.

why.It is an uncertain question, not a comma: This mistakes a command for an uncertain question.
This mistakes a command for a friendly wish.
This mistakes a spoken command for a written report.

activities.explanation: The falling tone usually shows an imperative command.

activities.prompt: A report says, “We arrived. The gate opened. We saw the evidence.” What should you notice?
options: The events happened earlier and are shown in order.
The events are happening now and shown in order.
The events happened earlier but are shown randomly.
The events are happening now and shown randomly.

why.The events are happening now and shown i: This wrongly treats a report as something happening now.
why.The events happened earlier but are show: This wrongly claims that the events are not in sequence.
why.The events are happening now and shown r: This gets both the time and the order wrong.

activities.explanation: A report is about past events and presents them in a proper sequence.

activities.context: During a school lesson, a student was preparing a formal letter about a legal case and a pencil case. The letter needed a subject line, and the student also wanted to make an anagram from the word case. At the dining table, Encyclopedia's family discussed a case. Encyclopedia solved the difficult case before his father finished dinner. The student learned that an encyclopedia is a book or set of books filled with facts.
activities.prompt: If Encyclopedia's father takes longer over dinner, what can the student conclude from the lesson?
options: Encyclopedia may solve the difficult case before his father finishes dinner.
He must wait until his father finishes dinner before he begins.
He will solve it only after his father has finished dinner.
He cannot solve it while the family is discussing cases.

why.He must wait until his father finishes d: Waiting until after dinner is not necessary.
why.He will solve it only after his father h: The lesson does not say that he can solve it only after dinner finishes.
why.He cannot solve it while the family is d: The family usually discusses cases at the dining table, and Encyclopedia can solve a difficult case before dinner is over.

activities.explanation: The lesson says that Encyclopedia can solve a difficult case before his father finishes dinner.

activities.context: During a school lesson, a student was preparing a formal letter about a legal case and a pencil case. The letter needed a subject line, and the student also wanted to make an anagram from the word case. At the dining table, Encyclopedia's family discussed a case. Encyclopedia solved the difficult case before his father finished dinner. The student learned that an encyclopedia is a book or set of books filled with facts.
activities.prompt: Which option is an anagram of the word "case"?
options: aces
case
pace
cast

why.case: It keeps the original order and does not make a new word.
why.pace: It replaces the letter s with p.
why.cast: It replaces the letter e with t.

activities.explanation: It uses the same letters in a different order.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Everyone else calls him Encyclopedia.
Reason (R): Only Encyclopedia's parents and teachers call him Leroy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The second statement identifies the only people who call him Leroy, so everyone else calls him Encyclopedia.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Encyclopedia's father finishes dinner before Encyclopedia solves a difficult case.
Reason (R): Encyclopedia can solve a difficult case before his father finishes dinner.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

activities.prompt: How does title case help in a formal letter, and how are anagrams and encyclopedias different?

It uses the same letters in a different order to make a new word or phrase. For example, "case" can be rearranged to make "aces," so "aces" is an anagram of "case," while "case" itself is not. An encyclopedia is also different: it is a book or set of books filled with facts. The lesson's ideas can be checked by asking what each expression means and how it is formed.

Rakesh grew taller and returned home to help his parents. When he came back, he was thinner but stronger. The tree grew another foot during the rains.

New shoots and leaves showed the tree's recovery.
Rakesh returned thinner but stronger.

That damage stayed permanent because it could not be repaired.

A praying-mantis

A butterfly

The cottage has become a home for warm weather.

The tree and cottage are facing a harsh winter.

why.The cottage has become a home for warm w: The mice seek shelter because of the winter conditions.
why.The field-mice have stopped needing any: Seeking shelter shows that they still need shelter.

The cherry tree has finished blooming for the year.
The cherry tree will grow no more blossoms.

why.The cherry tree has finished blooming fo: The blossom has just appeared, so this confuses beginning with ending.
why.The cherry tree will grow no more blosso: A new blossom suggests more life, not no future blossoms.

activities.explanation: A new blossom after winter suggests the tree is waking up.

activities.title: The Story of the Cherry Tree
activities.body: The cherry tree became taller. More blossoms appeared the following year. It soon became taller than Rakesh, then Grandfather. Bees came to feed on the nectar in the blossoms. Nectar is what the bees feed on. Tiny birds broke blossoms off. Small cherries grew that summer. Rakesh found the first cherries too sour. The birds feasted on the cherries. Grandfather called the tree special because they had planted it themselves.
keyPoints: More blossoms appeared the following year.
Bees fed on the nectar while tiny birds broke some blossoms.
The tree was special because they had planted it themselves.

activities.prompt: Their cherry tree grows taller than both Rakesh and Grandfather. How might they feel?

It later became taller than Grandfather too, so the growth continued.

They may feel proud because their own tree became so tall.

Grandfather

why.Bees broke every blossom before any cher: Bees fed on nectar, while the fact says birds broke the blossoms.
why.New blossoms appeared before the summer: More blossoms appeared the following year, after the summer cherries.

activities.context: Rakesh was six years old when he walked home from the Mussoorie bazaar after eating cherries. Grandfather ate one, while Rakesh quickly ate the other two. Rakesh had paid fifty paise for the bunch.
activities.prompt: If the dry cold winds near Rakesh’s home had not stopped most plants from growing, what change would be most likely?
options: More plants would be able to grow successfully close to the cottage.
Oak and deodar trees would grow on less sheltered slopes as well.
The narrow terraced fields would no longer be needed for farming.
All plants near the cottage would grow equally well.

why.Oak and deodar trees would grow on less: This is possible, but the case does not show that trees would spread to every slope.
why.The narrow terraced fields would no long: This mistakes improved plant growth for the removal of the family’s farming fields.
why.All plants near the cottage would grow e: This predicts that every plant would thrive, which is stronger than the original condition allows.

activities.explanation: Without the stopping effect of the cold winds, more nearby plants could grow properly.

activities.context: Rakesh was six years old when he walked home from the Mussoorie bazaar after eating cherries. The fruit had travelled from the Kashmir Valley and tasted a little sweet and a little sour. When he reached his grandfather’s cottage on the outskirts of Mussoorie, only three cherries remained. activities.prompt: If Rakesh had eaten one of the three cherries on the walk instead of leaving all three until the cottage, how would the sharing at the cottage have been likely to change?

The grandfather would take both, leaving nothing for Rakesh.
The grandfather would take none, leaving both to Rakesh.
Each would take one, and a third cherry would remain.

why.The grandfather would take both, leaving: This would give the grandfather both remaining cherries, unlike his sharing in the case.
why.The grandfather would take none, leaving: This would mean the grandfather did not take the cherry that he ate in the case.
why.Each would take one, and a third cherry: It miscounts two remaining cherries as allowing each person one and leaving an extra.

activities.explanation: Only two cherries would remain, so each person would most likely take one.

why.His parents grew maize, rice, and barley: His parents’ crops describe their work, not the reason for the arrangement.
why.Forests of oak and deodar grew on the mo: The sheltered forests form part of the setting, not the reason for the arrangement.

activities.explanation: It combines the lack of village schools with a place where Rakesh could stay.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Rakesh’s grandfather ate one of the three cherries that remained at the cottage.

activities.prompt: Explain how the climate near Rakesh’s home affected plants, farming, and the food he could find in Mussoorie.

why.Sow more mustard instead of planting the: This ignores the decision to plant the cherry seed.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

activities.prompt: How is asking whether a cherry seed is lucky different from actually putting that luck to use?

The main stem and the thin branches would have disappeared.
Grandfather would have said that the tree could not regrow.

why.The monsoon growth would have stopped im: The quick growth was linked to the monsoon season, not to the goat's absence.
why.The main stem and the thin branches woul: The stem and branches survived because the goat ate only the leaves.
why.Grandfather would have said that the tre: Grandfather described cherry trees as tough and able to grow again.

activities.explanation: Without the goat, the leaves would not have been eaten.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The cherry tree grew quickly during the monsoon season.
Reason (R): The monsoon rains came early that year.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The early arrival of the rains and the quick monsoon growth directly connect the two facts.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Rakesh stopped checking the tree every day because it seemed to grow slowly.
Reason (R): He stopped checking because the tree had already grown at least an inch and was growing quickly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The tree had grown at least an inch after a week or two, but Rakesh had stopped checking because its growth seemed slow.

activities.prompt: Explain how Rakesh's care and the monsoon affected the cherry tree's growth.
activities.answer: Rakesh cared for the tree by watering it from time to time and marking its base with pebbles for privacy. At first, the tree seemed to grow slowly, so Rakesh stopped checking it every day. After a week or two, however, it had gained at least an inch. The early monsoon rains were followed by rapid growth. Later, a goat ate every leaf, but the main stem and two slender branches remained. Grandfather's judgement was important: he described cherry trees as tough and able to grow again, so the damage did not mean the tree was finished.
points: Rakesh watered the tree from time to time.
Pebbles were used to give the tree privacy.
The tree gained at least an inch after a week or two.
It grew quickly during the monsoon season.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A woman cutting grass scrambled down a hillside in monsoon, her scythe swishing through foliage. She cut the cherry tree in two with one sweep. Grandfather followed and scolded her; the damage could not be repaired. The tree sent out several shoots with tender green leaves towards the end of the rainy season. Rakesh, eight and taller, returned thinner but stronger after helping his parents in the village. He sometimes watered the tree even when it rained.
activities.prompt: If the woman's scythe had stopped before it crossed the trunk, what could reasonably have happened?
options: The tree might have remained whole, avoiding the split shown in the case.
It would certainly have produced the same new shoots.
It would have grown exactly one more foot during the rains.
The original damage would still have been impossible to repair.

why.It would certainly have produced the sam: The new shoots appeared after the tree was cut, so they were not certain.
why.It would have grown exactly one more foo: The passage does not make further growth certain if the cut had been avoided.
why.The original damage would still have bee: Without the cut across the trunk, the same irreparable damage would not have occurred.

activities.explanation: Avoiding the cut could have prevented the damage that could not be repaired.

activities.context: A woman cutting grass scrambled down a hillside in monsoon, her scythe swishing through foliage. She cut the cherry tree in two with one sweep. Grandfather followed and scolded her; the damage could not be repaired. The tree sent out several shoots with tender green leaves towards the end of the rainy season. Rakesh, eight and taller, returned thinner but stronger after helping his parents in the village. He sometimes watered the tree even when it rained.
activities.prompt: Which conclusion about Rakesh's time in the village is supported?
options: His village work coincided with a slimmer build and greater physical strength.
His village work coincided with a slimmer build but weaker physical strength.
He grew taller while remaining as strong as before.
He returned with no change in his build or strength.

why.His village work coincided with a slimme: The passage states that he was stronger, not weaker, after returning.
why.He grew taller while remaining as strong: Only his build and strength are clearly said to have changed; his greater height is also mentioned.
why.He returned with no change in his build: The passage clearly records a difference in his physical condition.

activities.explanation: Rakesh returned from the village thinner but stronger.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The damaged cherry tree showed signs of recovery.
Reason (R): New shoots with tender green leaves and another foot of growth provided evidence of recovery.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the new growth explains why the tree showed recovery.

lessons.title: Feathered Friend: A Pet in Space

activities.prompt: Could a little bird learn to fly without gravity?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Sven and Claribel
activities.body: No rule has ever forbidden pets in a space station. Sven was one of the best construction workers. He collected girders in free fall, meaning they floated around. He fused, or joined, pieces that fitted exactly. Then he stepped back and admired the work. He brought Claribel, a yellow canary, from Earth. Claribel floated, stayed still, flew a backward loop, and learned to operate without any weight. She became the station's pet.
keyPoints: No regulation has ever forbidden people from keeping pets.
Sven fused pieces that fitted exactly and admired the work.
Claribel flew a backward loop and operated without weight.
activities.explanation: The lesson connects Sven's building work with his unusual pet.

activities.prompt: Can one small canary become a pet for a whole space station?
steps: No regulation banned pets, so bringing Claribel broke no stated rule.
Sven brought her because he wanted to test wings without weight.
Claribel learned to float, so her backward loop showed her skill.
Therefore, Sven's test worked, and Claribel became the whole station's pet.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who did Sven bring to the space station?
options: Claribel
A hummingbird
A girder
Sven
activities.explanation: Sven smuggled Claribel, the small yellow canary, from Earth.

activities.prompt: Claribel was a small yellow canary.
activities.explanation: Yes! Claribel was a small yellow canary who floated in the air.

activities.prompt: Sven collected ______ that floated around in free fall.
activities.hint: These were the building pieces that Sven collected.
activities.explanation: Sven collected girders that floated around in free fall.

activities.prompt: Why did Sven bring Claribel to the station?
options: He wanted to watch a bird use wings without any weight.
He wanted to watch a bird join together the floating girders.
He wanted to watch a bird fuse together pieces for building work.
He wanted to watch a bird collect pieces for Sven's work.
activities.explanation: Sven wanted to see how a bird would use its wings without any weight.

activities.prompt: Put Sven's building actions in order.
items: Step back and admire the handiwork
activities.explanation: Sven collected the pieces first, joined them next, and admired the result last.

activities.prompt: Sven fused pieces together even when they did not fit exactly.
activities.explanation: Good try! He fused pieces only when they fitted exactly into place.

activities.prompt: You watch Sven test wings without weight. How does he likely feel?
options: angry at the bird
afraid of the station
curious about the result
sad about the test

why.angry at the bird: Anger does not fit Sven's wish to learn from Claribel.
why.afraid of the station: Bringing her to the station shows interest, not fear.
why.sad about the test: He had an exciting question, so sadness does not fit.

activities.explanation: His wish to learn how wings work shows curiosity.

activities.prompt: You watch Claribel learn to operate without gravity. She flies a backward loop. What does this show?
options: She was afraid to fly
She needed help to float
She could control her flight
She could not use wings

why.She was afraid to fly: A backward loop shows confidence, not fear of flying.
why.She needed help to float: She flew by herself, so help is not needed.
why.She could not use wings: The loop proves that she did use her wings.

activities.explanation: The backward loop shows that she could control her flight.

activities.prompt: A girder floats around Sven in free fall. What does that mean?
options: floating with no downward weight
falling down a steep stair
resting on a strong shelf
moving after one hard push

why.falling down a steep stair: This is a space station, not a place with a stair.
why.resting on a strong shelf: The girders floated around, so they were not resting.
why.moving after one hard push: Their floating was described as free fall, not a push.

activities.explanation: Free fall here means floating without downward weight.

activities.prompt: You watch workers admire their fused pieces. How do they likely feel?
options: angry at the pieces
afraid of the result
bored by the work
proud of their skill

why.angry at the pieces: Admiring their handiwork does not show anger at the pieces.
why.afraid of the result: They admired the result, so there is no sign of fear.
why.bored by the work: They took time to admire the work, so boredom does not fit.

activities.explanation: Admiring their handiwork suggests pride in their skill.
