lessons.title: Feathered Friend: The Canary Saves the Crew

activities.prompt: How could a tiny bird help keep a space-station crew safe?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Claribel’s Warning
activities.body: The crew floated in permanent sunlight, so they had no day or night. Sven found a tiny bundle of yellow feathers. The cook held Claribel against his ear to listen closely. Claribel revived when she received oxygen. She collapsed again soon after the oxygen mask was removed. Without Claribel, the crew would soon have been slightly dead.
keyPoints: Permanent sunlight left the crew without day or night.
Claribel revived after receiving oxygen.
She collapsed again after the oxygen mask was removed.
activities.explanation: Claribel’s warning gave the crew a chance to stay safe.

activities.prompt: How could one small bird help a whole crew in danger?
steps: The second circuit was not connected, and the only alarm had failed.
So the crew had no working alarm to warn them.
Miners used canaries for gas warnings, so Claribel could warn the crew.
Thus Claribel could save the crew from being slightly dead.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Two Ways to Stay Safe
activities.body: Canaries were useful warning birds. Miners carried them underground so birdsong could warn them about gas. On the station, the second alarm circuit was not yet connected. The only connected alarm had failed. One part of the air purifier had also frozen. In this lesson, doubly safeguarded means protected in two ways. Hearing Claribel’s birdsong would show that the crew had this double protection.
keyPoints: Miners used canaries to warn them about gas.
The only connected alarm had failed.
Claribel’s birdsong showed double protection.
activities.explanation: Claribel provided warning when the station’s alarms could not help.

activities.prompt: Why did the crew have no day or night?
options: Permanent sunlight kept them in endless light.
Earth’s shadow covered the station all day.
An eclipse changed each day into night.
Miners’ gas alarms stopped the sunlight.
activities.explanation: The crew floated in permanent sunlight. This light stayed the same all the time.

activities.prompt: Miners once carried ______ underground to warn them about gas.
activities.hint: These birds could warn miners about gas.
activities.explanation: Miners carried canaries underground. The birds helped warn them about gas.

activities.prompt: The cook held Claribel against his ear to listen closely.
activities.explanation: Yes, the cook held Claribel against his ear. He was listening closely to her.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its matching detail.
pairs: Permanent sunlight with no day or night
A tiny bundle of yellow feathers
activities.explanation: Each detail comes from a different event in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What happened soon after Claribel revived?
options: The oxygen mask was removed.
The second alarm was connected.
The air purifier began working.
Earth’s shadow reached the station.
activities.explanation: Claribel collapsed again soon after the oxygen mask was removed.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Sven found a tiny bundle of yellow feathers.
The cook held Claribel against his ear.
Claribel was given oxygen and revived.
activities.explanation: This is the order of events described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Sven found tiny yellow feathers. Miners once used canaries underground for gas warnings. Why might Sven hope to find a canary?
options: He hoped it could warn the crew about gas.
He hoped it could repair the failed alarm.
He hoped it could connect the alarm circuit.
He hoped it could bring back sunlight.

why.He hoped it could repair the failed alar: Wrong: a canary gives warnings, but it cannot repair alarms.
why.He hoped it could connect the alarm circ: Wrong: a canary cannot connect an alarm circuit.
Wrong: a canary cannot bring sunlight back to a station.

activities.explanation: Right: canaries had warned miners about gas.

activities.prompt: Claribel collapsed again after her oxygen mask was removed. How might the cook have felt?
options: Cheerful, because Claribel had revived once.
Worried, because Claribel still needed oxygen.
Calm, because Claribel was safe without oxygen.
Cross, because Claribel would not sing.

why.Cheerful, because Claribel had revived o: Wrong: a brief revival did not mean Claribel was safe.
why.Calm, because Claribel was safe without: Wrong: collapsing again showed she was not safe without oxygen.
Wrong: nothing showed that the cook felt cross.

activities.explanation: Right: her second collapse showed that oxygen was still needed.

activities.prompt: The cook held Claribel against his ear and listened closely. What did he likely hope to learn?
options: Whether Claribel could sing a clear song.
Whether Claribel was still breathing normally.
Whether Claribel had seen sunlight outside.
Whether Claribel liked the crew very much.

why.Whether Claribel could sing a clear song: Wrong: the cook was checking her breathing, not her singing.
why.Whether Claribel had seen sunlight outsi: Wrong: listening closely did not show whether she saw sunlight.
why.Whether Claribel liked the crew very muc: Wrong: the cook was checking her breathing, not her likes.

activities.explanation: Right: listening closely could show if Claribel was still breathing.

activities.prompt: The station had a rare eclipse. Part of the air purifier had frozen. Without Claribel, the crew would soon have been slightly dead. Why was Claribel important to the crew?
options: She could repair the frozen air purifier.
She could warn the crew about gas.
She could connect the second alarm circuit.
She could bring sunlight back to the station.

why.She could repair the frozen air purifier: Wrong: Claribel could warn about gas, but she could not repair machinery.
why.She could connect the second alarm circu: Wrong: connecting a circuit was a job for people, not a canary.
why.She could bring sunlight back to the sta: Wrong: bringing sunlight was not what a canary could do.

activities.explanation: Right: canaries gave gas warnings, and her birdsong showed a doubly safeguarded crew.

lessons.title: Magnifying Glass: Small Things Become Wonders

activities.prompt: What wonders could a magnifying glass reveal in ordinary things?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Small Wonders Under the Glass
activities.body: A round magnifying glass shows a chalk scrap filled with myriad shells. Myriad means a very large number. An inch of moss becomes a forest with flowers and trees. A water drop seems like a busy hive of bees. The deft spider shoots woven web-silk and has fierce, tiger-like claws. Deft means skilful. Web-silk is the silk the spider weaves. Through lenses, the moon seems close enough for a walk.
keyPoints: The magnifying glass makes tiny things look marvellous.
Nature becomes magical under the lens.
The moon seems close enough for a walk.
activities.explanation: The glass turns tiny wonders into magical sights.

activities.prompt: Why does the speaker look closely at tiny things in nature?
steps: The round magnifying glass makes nature seem magical to the speaker.
This happens because the glass makes tiny things look marvellous.
So small details become surprising when viewed through the lens.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Glass Beyond the Glass
activities.body: Small objects can become huge wonders under the glass. Shells fill a piece of chalk, while moss becomes a flowered forest. A drop of water looks like a hive of bees. The spider shoots out woven web-silk, and its fierce claws look tiger-like. The glass seems to surpass itself. Even the moon appears near enough for a walk.
keyPoints: Tiny objects reveal new wonders.
The glass seems to surpass itself.
The moon appears close through lenses.
activities.explanation: The lesson celebrates the glass's marvellous power.

activities.prompt: What does the round magnifying glass do to nature?
options: It makes nature seem magical.
It makes nature look dull.
It makes nature disappear.
It makes nature lose its colour.
activities.explanation: The speaker uses the round glass to make nature seem magical.

activities.prompt: A drop of water looks like a quiet, empty pool.
activities.explanation: A drop of water looks like a hive of bees under the glass.

activities.prompt: A scrap of chalk contains a ______ of shells.
activities.hint: This word means a very large number.
activities.explanation: The chalk contains a myriad of shells.

activities.prompt: Match each small thing with its magnified wonder.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a small thing becoming a marvellous sight.

activities.prompt: What does the spider shoot out?
options: Web-silk
Chalk shells
Moss flowers
Water bees
activities.explanation: The deft spider shoots out woven web-silk.

activities.prompt: The spider has fierce, tiger-like ______.
activities.hint: The spider uses these sharp parts.
activities.explanation: The spider has fierce, tiger-like claws.

activities.prompt: At school, a child looks through the round magnifying glass. Tiny things turn marvellous before the child's eyes. How does the child most likely feel?
options: excited and amazed
bored and tired
angry and afraid
sure and calm

why.bored and tired: Feeling bored ignores the child's wonder at tiny things.
why.angry and afraid: Feeling angry or afraid is not suggested by the magical view.
why.sure and calm: Feeling sure and calm does not fit the child's surprise.

activities.explanation: The marvellous view naturally causes excitement and amazement.

activities.prompt: The glass makes tiny things marvellous and seems to surpass itself. What does "surpass itself" suggest?
options: It reveals wonders beyond a glass's usual role.
It makes small things turn back into tiny things.
It proves that nature has no magical sights.
It makes the glass lose its power to see.

why.It makes small things turn back into tin: This mistake takes "surpass" to mean making things smaller again.
why.It proves that nature has no magical sig: This mistake treats surprising sights as proof that nature is ordinary.
why.It makes the glass lose its power to see: This mistake misses the glass's special power to magnify tiny wonders.

activities.explanation: The glass does more than expected because it reveals marvellous tiny things.

activities.prompt: A child examines one inch of moss through the magnifying glass. It looks like a forest with flowers and trees. What wonder is the child noticing?
options: Small things can show large scenes.
Real trees grow inside the moss.
The moss really is a forest.
The glass makes every forest tiny.

This mistake takes a "looks like" image to mean real trees.
This mistake mistakes a seeming forest for a real forest.
This mistake reverses the glass's power to make tiny things seem large.

activities.explanation: The tiny moss seems like a whole forest, so small things can show large scenes.

activities.prompt: A child watches the spider shoot out woven web-silk. The spider also has fierce, tiger-like claws. What does this description make the spider seem?
options: Skillful and a little frightening.
Calm and always completely harmless.
Small and quite unable to act.
Simple and very easy to control.

This mistake ignores the fierce, tiger-like claws.
This mistake overlooks the spider's quick and skillful action.
This mistake focuses on control, but the description shows wildness and skill.

activities.explanation: The deft web-silk shows skill, while the fierce claws suggest something frightening.

activities.prompt: A child looks through lenses at the moon. The moon seems close enough for a walk. What does this imply about the lenses?
options: They make far things seem near.
They make near things seem far.
They show the moon as very small.
They keep every moon out of sight.

This mistake reverses the meaning of "close enough for a walk."
This mistake focuses on size, but the line is about nearness.
This mistake contradicts the image because the moon seems visible and near.

activities.explanation: A moon close enough for a walk means the lenses make far things seem near.

lessons.title: Magnifying Glass: Tools for Looking and Discovering

activities.prompt: How can tiny tools help us see bigger, farther, and clearer?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Tools That Help Us See
activities.body: Children with low vision can benefit from several types of visual aid. Magnifying spectacles help with reading and threading a needle. Stand magnifiers rest above objects, so they work without hands. Hand-held magnifiers may have lights. Telescopes help people see objects or signs far away. India’s largest telescope for studying celestial objects is in Nainital, Uttarakhand. The Indian Astronomical Observatory is a high-altitude astronomy station.
keyPoints: Stand magnifiers work above objects without hands.
Telescopes help people see faraway objects or signs.
Observatories and magnifiers are tools for discovery.
activities.explanation: These tools help with reading, threading, and seeing far away.

activities.prompt: Riya has low vision and must thread a small needle. Which visual aid should she choose?
steps: Low vision can benefit from visual aids, so she should try one.
Magnifying spectacles help with reading and threading a needle.
This matches her needle task, so magnifying spectacles are the best choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which tool rests above an object and works without hands?
options: Stand magnifier
Hand-held magnifier
Magnifying spectacles
Telescope
activities.explanation: A stand magnifier rests above objects and works without hands.

activities.prompt: Which tool helps you see an object or sign far away?
options: Stand magnifier
Hand-held magnifier
Telescope
Magnifying spectacles
activities.explanation: Telescopes help people see objects or signs far away.

activities.prompt: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II built Jantar Mantar in ______.
activities.hint: Use the year given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Jantar Mantar was built in 1724 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its correct answer.
pairs: Built in 1724 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II
India’s largest telescope for studying celestial objects
activities.explanation: Each clue points to a place, model, telescope, or structure.

activities.prompt: What did Āryabhaṭa propose?
options: A high-altitude astronomy station
A hand-held magnifier with built-in lights
Visual aids for children with low vision
A heliocentric model of the solar system
activities.explanation: Āryabhaṭa proposed a heliocentric model before Copernicus.

activities.prompt: India’s largest telescope for studying celestial objects is in ______, Uttarakhand.
activities.hint: Use the place given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: India’s largest telescope for studying celestial objects is in Nainital.

activities.prompt: Riya has low vision. She wants help with reading and threading a needle. Which visual aid should she use?
options: Use magnifying spectacles for both tasks.
Use stand magnifiers for both tasks.
Use hand-held magnifiers for both tasks.
Use telescopes for both tasks.

This confuses a hands-free magnifier with magnifying spectacles.
This chooses a magnifier by its light feature, not its stated use.
This uses a tool for far-away objects on close tasks.

activities.explanation: Magnifying spectacles help with reading and threading a needle.

activities.prompt: Neel is shaping clay with both hands. He needs to see tiny details. Which tool fits best?
options: Choose a stand magnifier that needs no hands.
Choose a hand-held magnifier that needs no hands.
Choose a magnifying glass that needs no hands.
Choose a telescope that needs no hands.

why.Choose a hand-held magnifier that needs: This confuses a hand-held tool with a hands-free magnifier.
why.Choose a magnifying glass that needs no: This assumes every magnifying glass is held in one hand.
This chooses a far-viewing tool for seeing tiny details.

activities.explanation: A stand magnifier rests above objects and works without hands.

activities.prompt: Sam holds a small tool in a dark cupboard. Which feature should he look for?
options: A hand-held magnifier with a built-in light.
A stand magnifier with a built-in light.
Magnifying spectacles with a built-in light.
A telescope with a built-in light.

The fact gives this light feature to hand-held magnifiers.
why.Magnifying spectacles with a built-in li: The fact does not say magnifying spectacles have built-in lights.
The fact gives this light feature to hand-held magnifiers.

activities.explanation: Hand-held magnifiers may have lights built into them.

activities.prompt: One visitor wants India's largest telescope for studying celestial objects. Another needs a high-altitude astronomy station. Which plan is correct?
options: The first goes to Nainital; the second visits the Indian Astronomical Observatory.
The first visits the observatory; the second goes to Nainital.
The first goes to Nainital; the second visits the James Webb Space Telescope.
The first visits Jantar Mantar; the second goes to Nainital.

why.The first visits the observatory; the se: This swaps the places connected with the two needs.
why.The first goes to Nainital; the second v: The James Webb Space Telescope is not described as a high-altitude station.

lessons.title: Bibha Chowdhuri: A Pioneer in Indian Science

activities.prompt: What discoveries can grow from one woman’s curiosity about the universe?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A scientific pioneer
activities.body: Bibha Chowdhuri was India’s first woman physicist. She became the first Indian woman to excel in high-energy particle physics. Born in Kolkata in 1913, she began her academic journey at the University of Manchester in 1945. Patrick M.S. Blackett guided her research into cosmic rays. Her greatest discovery was the pi-meson, a subatomic particle. She also became the first woman faculty member at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research.
keyPoints: India’s first woman physicist
Research into cosmic rays and the pi-meson
First woman faculty member at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research
activities.explanation: These achievements show Bibha Chowdhuri’s brilliant work in physics.

activities.prompt: A student sees Bibha’s name on a renamed star. Why is she called a science pioneer?
steps: As India’s first woman physicist, she opened a path for women.
Her success in high-energy particle physics showed strong research skills.
A Nobel nomination shows that her scientific work drew serious recognition.
Later honours show why India remembers her as a science pioneer.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In ______, Bibha began her academic journey at the University of Manchester.
activities.hint: Think of the year when her academic journey began.
activities.explanation: She began her academic journey at Manchester in 1945.

activities.prompt: Bibha Chowdhuri was India’s first woman physicist.
activities.explanation: Yes, she was India’s first woman physicist.

activities.prompt: Bibha Chowdhuri was born in Kolkata in 1945.
activities.explanation: She was born in Kolkata in 1913. In 1945, she began her academic journey.

activities.prompt: What was Bibha Chowdhuri’s greatest discovery?
options: the pi-meson
the Nobel Prize
the cosmic rays
a renamed star
activities.explanation: Her greatest discovery was the pi-meson. It was a subatomic particle.

activities.prompt: Match each person or place with the linked achievement.
pairs: Nominated her for a Nobel Prize
Called the Rocket Woman of India
activities.explanation: Each person or place is linked to an important part of the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put Bibha Chowdhuri’s milestones in the correct order.
items: Nominated for a Nobel Prize in 1950
activities.explanation: The dates help you follow Bibha Chowdhuri’s life from 1913 to 2020.

activities.prompt: Bibha was India’s first woman physicist. She also excelled in high-energy particle physics. What does her example show?
options: She opened paths for women in important science fields.
She was the only woman working in Indian physics.
She had worked in every branch of Indian science.
She became important only after India’s space work began.

why.She was the only woman working in Indian: First does not mean only; other women could follow her.
why.She had worked in every branch of Indian: Two physics achievements do not mean she worked in every branch.
why.She became important only after India’s: It wrongly links her physics distinction with later space work.

activities.explanation: Being first and excelling show that she opened paths for women.

activities.prompt: Ritu Karidhal Srivastava was called the “Rocket Woman of India”. More than 50 women contributed to Chandrayaan-3. What do these facts suggest?
options: Women have shared important roles in India’s science work.
One woman handled all of the country’s rocket research.
Women joined Chandrayaan-3 only after the mission ended.
The Rocket Woman led every woman working on Chandrayaan-3.

why.One woman handled all of the country’s r: A title for one woman does not mean she did all rocket research.
why.Women joined Chandrayaan-3 only after th: Contributing means working on the mission, not joining after it ended.
why.The Rocket Woman led every woman working: The nickname does not prove that she led every mission contributor.

activities.explanation: The nickname and many contributors both show women’s important roles.

activities.prompt: In 1945, Bibha began at the University of Manchester. Blackett guided her cosmic-ray research. How might she have felt about this support?
options: Hopeful about making progress in her chosen research.
Sure that Blackett would nominate her for a Nobel Prize.
Happy that a government chair had already been named.
Certain that a star would soon carry her name.

why.Sure that Blackett would nominate her fo: Schrödinger, not Blackett, sent the 1950 Nobel nomination.
why.Happy that a government chair had alread: The 2020 chair came later; it was not already there.
why.Certain that a star would soon carry her: The 2019 star honour came later and was not caused by guidance.

activities.explanation: Blackett’s guidance could make Bibha hopeful about research progress.

activities.prompt: Bibha’s greatest discovery was the pi-meson, a subatomic particle. What does “greatest” suggest here?
options: It was the most important discovery among her work.
It was the largest particle she had ever found.
It was the first discovery made by any Indian scientist.
It was the discovery that won her a Nobel Prize.

why.It was the largest particle she had ever: It mistakes importance for physical size.
why.It was the first discovery made by any I: It mistakes importance for being the earliest discovery.
why.It was the discovery that won her a Nobe: She was nominated for a Nobel Prize, but she did not win.

activities.explanation: Greatest means most important, not biggest or first.

activities.prompt: Erwin Schrödinger nominated Bibha for a Nobel Prize in 1950. What can we safely conclude?
options: Her work had earned significant scientific recognition.
She had already won the Nobel Prize in 1950.
The Nobel Prize committee had chosen her as its winner.
Her work was unimportant, so the nomination meant little.

why.She had already won the Nobel Prize in 1: A nomination is not the same as winning the prize.
why.The Nobel Prize committee had chosen her: The nomination came from Schrödinger; it did not name a winner.
why.Her work was unimportant, so the nominat: The nomination shows recognition, not that her work was unimportant.

activities.explanation: A Nobel nomination shows that her work received serious attention.

activities.prompt: In 2019, the IAU renamed a star for Bibha. In 2020, India declared a chair professorship for her. What do both acts show?
options: Her scientific legacy was honoured in lasting and public ways.
She had led every Indian institute where women worked.
Her Nobel nomination had already created both honours.
These honours began her scientific research work.

why.She had led every Indian institute where: First at one institute does not mean leading every Indian institute.
why.Her Nobel nomination had already created: The 1950 nomination did not create the 2019 star or 2020 chair.
why.These honours began her scientific resea: These honours came later; they did not begin her research.

activities.explanation: The star and chair publicly honour her lasting scientific legacy.

activities.title: How AR, VR and Awards Help Learning
activities.body: Augmented reality, or AR, adds digital elements to a person’s environment. It usually works through a smartphone camera. Virtual reality, or VR, replaces the real world with a simulated one. AR and VR help students understand difficult ideas. NCERT’s e-Pathshala AR App supports learning through experiments and turns passive listeners into active learners. The Digital India vision uses technology to empower sectors. Awards recognise important scientific and technological contributions.
keyPoints: AR adds digital elements, while VR replaces the real world with a simulated one.
The e-Pathshala App encourages experiments and active learning.
Digital India and science awards support technology and scientific contributions.
activities.explanation: New technology can make learning more active and help recognise important contributions.

activities.prompt: Mina wants to learn about a volcano, but she cannot touch one. How can AR or VR help her?
steps: Mina chooses AR, because it adds digital elements to her environment.
She uses a smartphone camera, because AR usually works through one.

Thus, AR and VR let her interact with things she cannot touch.

activities.prompt: In VR, Meera’s real room disappears. A simulated volcano appears instead. What does “simulated” suggest about the volcano?

It is a drawing inside a science book.
It is not real; it is made digitally.
It is a volcano that she can touch.

This mistake treats the simulated volcano as a real place.

activities.prompt: NCERT’s app lets students experiment instead of only reading and memorising. How can Arjun become an active learner?

He can only listen to the teacher.
He can copy the textbook without trying.
He can wait for instructions before doing anything.

This mistake thinks listening alone makes someone active.
This mistake thinks copying without trying is active learning.

activities.explanation: This is right because experimenting turns a passive listener into an active learner.

activities.prompt: How did Claribel’s collapse show the difference between temporary revival and lasting protection?
activities.answer: Claribel revived when she was given oxygen, but she collapsed again soon after the oxygen mask was removed. This showed that a brief recovery was not enough to keep her safe. Lasting protection would require Claribel to remain alive as well as reliable alarm protection, and birdsong would show that the crew was doubly safeguarded.

why.The forest-like scene would remain becau: The glass changes the view, not the chalk itself.
why.The bee-like scene would take the place: Lowering the glass would not replace the shells with a bee-like scene.
